Below the threshold, the maximum contagion rate scales as ν_max ∝ φ^(1/2), meaning transmission is governed by encounter frequency. Above the threshold, universal scaling is lost and protection dominates epidemic control, with strongest suppression at low densities.
AI.conclusion: Microscopic active-matter models provide a powerful framework for studying epidemic dynamics beyond well-mixed assumptions, showing that spatial organization and individual protection jointly determine contagion dynamics.

title: Observation of g-wave altermagnetic multipole
summary: Over the past few years, altermagnets have emerged as a new class of collinear magnets with broken time-reversal symmetry, offering novel opportunities for spintronics beyond conventional magnets. Rather than from net magnetization, as in ferromagnets, the unconventional time-reversal symmetry breaking of altermagnets originates from antiferroic magnetic dipoles locked to higher-order multipoles. Here we report the direct visualization of a $g$-wave altermagnetic multipole in the canonical altermagnet CrSb. Combining high-energy synchrotron X-ray diffraction with valence electron density (VED) analysis, we uncover a pronounced directional anisotropy of the VED distribution alternating between Cr sublattices. This evidences the antiferroic order of electric hexadecapoles predicted in $g$-wave altermagnets. Its coexistence with antiferroic magnetic dipoles induces ferroic magnetic multipoles, as probed by polarized neutron diffraction. We further identify a microscopic model of altermagnetism that directly relates the $g$-wave multipole and the $g$-wave spin splitting. Through direct observation and quantification of multipoles, this study provides a real-space fingerprint of altermagnetism and establishes a general probe of hidden multipole order in quantum materials.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the direct visualization of a g-wave altermagnetic multipole in the canonical altermagnet CrSb using high-energy synchrotron X-ray diffraction and valence electron density analysis. The researchers observed antiferroic order of electric hexadecapoles coexisting with antiferroic magnetic dipoles, inducing ferroic magnetic multipoles verified by polarized neutron diffraction. They establish a microscopic model linking g-wave multipoles to g-wave spin splitting, providing a real-space fingerprint of altermagnetism and a general probe for hidden multipole order in quantum materials.
AI.motivation: Altermagnets represent a new class of collinear magnets with unconventional time-reversal symmetry breaking originating from antiferroic magnetic dipoles locked to higher-order multipoles, rather than net magnetization. The researchers aimed to directly visualize and quantify these elusive higher-order multipoles in a canonical altermagnet, providing experimental evidence for the theoretically predicted multipole order.
AI.method: The study combines high-energy synchrotron X-ray diffraction with valence electron density (VED) analysis to map the directional anisotropy of electron density alternating between Cr sublattices. This reveals antiferroic order of electric hexadecapoles. Polarized neutron diffraction was used to probe the coexistence of antiferroic magnetic dipoles and the resulting ferroic magnetic multipoles. A microscopic model was then developed to relate the g-wave multipole to g-wave spin splitting.
AI.result: The researchers directly observed a pronounced directional anisotropy in the valence electron density distribution that alternates between Cr sublattices in CrSb, evidencing antiferroic electric hexadecapole order characteristic of g-wave altermagnets. The coexistence of these electric multipoles with antiferroic magnetic dipoles induces ferroic magnetic multipoles confirmed by polarized neutron diffraction. A microscopic model directly links the g-wave multipole order to g-wave spin splitting.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the first direct real-space fingerprint of altermagnetism through multipole visualization and quantification. It establishes a general experimental probe for detecting hidden multipole order in quantum materials, advancing fundamental understanding and potential spintronic applications of altermagnets.

title: A Probability Model for Pentagonal Prism Dice Rolls
summary: In the realm of probability theory and game design, the study of dice probabilities plays a crucial role. The featured dice are usually fair, so their probabilities can be predicted without rolling the dice. Pentagonal prismatic dice are not fair. Hence, the probabilities are more complicated. Our mathematical model is naturally derived from both the geometric properties of the dice and empirical evidence. Dice of varying sizes but with constant volume were designed. Using a 3D printer with 100 percent infill, the dice were printed and prepared. A machine that simulates dropping dice through a dice tower onto a hard surface was used to obtain about 41,000 results. From these data, a statistical model was constructed that gives probabilities of dice with varying height-to-radius ratios. The formula for the model is based on the centroid solid angle, but with two adjustment parameters due to varying energy and other requirements to transition between different resting aspects. Within the range of height-to-radius ratios tested, the data are within reasonable statistical error of the model.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a statistical model for predicting the landing probabilities of non-fair pentagonal prismatic dice by combining geometric properties (centroid solid angle) with empirical data collected from ~41,000 drops of 3D-printed dice of varying height-to-radius ratios but constant volume.
AI.motivation: While fair dice probabilities can be predicted without rolling, pentagonal prismatic dice are inherently unfair, making their probabilities more complicated. The authors aim to create a mathematical model that accounts for the geometry and empirical behavior of such dice.
AI.method: Dice of varying sizes with constant volume were designed and 3D-printed with 100% infill. A machine simulating dice tower drops onto a hard surface collected approximately 41,000 results. A statistical model was constructed based on the centroid solid angle, modified by two adjustment parameters that account for varying energy and transition requirements between resting aspects, with the height-to-radius ratio as the key variable.
AI.result: Within the tested range of height-to-radius ratios, the model's predictions align with the empirical data within reasonable statistical error.
AI.conclusion: The proposed model, combining centroid solid angle geometry with two empirical adjustment parameters, successfully predicts the outcome probabilities of pentagonal prismatic dice across the tested parameter range.

title: Physics-informed Learning for Orbital Uncertainty Propagation with Error Bounds
summary: The Fokker-Planck partial differential equation (FP-PDE) governs uncertainty evolution in stochastic dynamical systems. In orbital dynamics, solving the FP-PDE is challenging because of nonlinear motion, high-dimensional states, and large space-time domains. We develop a physics-informed neural network (PINN) approach that approximates the FP-PDE solution as a single space-time probability density, while also quantifying its worst-case approximation error. This approach is, in principle, independent of the choice of state coordinates and neural network architecture. Specifically, to enforce probability density function (PDF) properties into the neural network, we design a Physics-informed Gaussian mixture model (PINN-GMM). Then a companion error PINN learns the dynamics of the approximation error and yields time-dependent bounds that define an ambiguity set of PDFs. This ambiguity set enables rigorous computation of upper and lower bounds on event probabilities through tractable linear programs. Numerical studies on illustrative 1D examples and several 4D--6D orbital test cases demonstrate accurate uncertainty propagation, correct and informative error bounds, and improved reliability over common uncertainty-propagation baseline methods (Gaussian approximation, unscented transform, and Gaussian mixture model). Constructing the PINN-GMM requires offline training, making it costlier than the baseline approximations; once trained, however, a single forward pass returns the density at any time in sub-millisecond time $(0.16~\mathrm{ms}$ in our implementation).

AI.tldr: This paper develops a physics-informed neural network (PINN) approach to solve the Fokker-Planck PDE for uncertainty propagation in orbital dynamics. The method uses a Gaussian mixture model architecture (PINN-GMM) to enforce PDF properties, plus a companion error-PINN that learns approximation error dynamics to provide rigorous time-dependent bounds on event probabilities via ambiguity sets and linear programs.
AI.motivation: Solving the Fokker-Planck PDE for uncertainty evolution in stochastic orbital dynamical systems is highly challenging due to nonlinear motion, high-dimensional state spaces, and large space-time domains. Existing uncertainty-propagation baselines (e.g., Gaussian approximation, unscented transform, GMM) provide limited accuracy or reliability for such problems.
AI.method: The approach approximates the FP-PDE solution as a single space-time probability density using a PINN with a Gaussian-mixture-model structure (PINN-GMM) to inherently enforce PDF properties. A companion error-PINN learns the dynamics of the approximation error and produces time-dependent bounds forming an ambiguity set of PDFs. This ambiguity set enables rigorous upper/lower bounds on event probabilities through tractable linear programs.
AI.result: Numerical studies on 1D illustrative cases and 4D-6D orbital test cases show accurate uncertainty propagation, correct and informative error bounds, and improved reliability compared to baseline methods (Gaussian approximation, unscented transform, and Gaussian mixture model). Once trained offline, a single forward pass yields the density in sub-millisecond time (0.16 ms).
AI.conclusion: The PINN-GMM with companion error-PINN is coordinate-system and architecture independent, offering rigorous, time-dependent uncertainty quantification with computational efficiency at inference time. The primary trade-off is the offline training cost, which exceeds baseline approximations.

title: All-dry processing of 3C-SiC nanomechanical string resonators for extreme aspect ratios and high intrinsic quality factor
summary: Conventional fabrication of suspended nanomechanical resonators typically relies on wet-chemical process steps and critical point drying, which can compromise sample yield and cleanliness. Here, we present an all-dry fabrication process for strongly stressed 3C-SiC nanomechanical string resonators that entirely avoids wet-chemical etching and cleaning. Using a negative-tone electron-beam resist as an etch mask and a three-step reactive-ion etching process for both structuring and release, we achieve high fabrication yield, clean suspended structures, and extreme aspect ratios of 8.500. We perform full mechanical characterization of the resulting doubly-clamped nanostring resonators, and establish a benchmark intrinsic quality factor for dissipation-diluted 3C-SiC of Qintr = 4.200.

AI.tldr: An all-dry fabrication process using negative-tone e-beam resist and three-step reactive-ion etching enables fabrication of strongly stressed 3C-SiC nanomechanical string resonators with high yield, clean surfaces, aspect ratios up to 8,500, and a benchmark intrinsic quality factor of Qintr = 4,200 for dissipation-diluted 3C-SiC.
AI.motivation: Conventional fabrication of suspended nanomechanical resonators relies on wet-chemical process steps and critical point drying, which compromise sample yield and cleanliness. The authors aim to develop a fully dry fabrication route to overcome these limitations.
AI.method: The fabrication utilizes a negative-tone electron-beam resist as an etch mask combined with a three-step reactive-ion etching process for both structuring and release, entirely avoiding wet-chemical etching and cleaning. Complete mechanical characterization of the resulting doubly-clamped nanostring resonators is performed.
AI.result: The process achieves high fabrication yield, clean suspended structures, and extreme aspect ratios of 8,500. Mechanical characterization establishes a benchmark intrinsic quality factor of Qintr = 4,200 for dissipation-diluted 3C-SiC resonators.
AI.conclusion: The all-dry fabrication process successfully produces high-quality, strongly stressed 3C-SiC nanomechanical string resonators with record intrinsic quality factors, offering a clean and high-yield alternative to conventional wet-chemical fabrication methods.

title: Latent unified smooth Hamiltonians for excited state chemistry
comment: 24 pages main, 7 pages supplement, 4 figures main, 6 figures supplement, 2 tables supplement
summary: We describe a neural network architecture and training procedure designed to model electronic ground and excited states of arbitrary molecular systems. By indirectly learning a latent, implicit basis representation of the electronic-state Hamiltonian, the model offers a unified treatment of multiple electronic states, conical intersections, and non-adiabatic couplings. The formalism can be further extended to learn consistent latent representations of additional operators such as transition dipole moments, for example. To demonstrate the general capabilities of our architecture, we train and evaluate networks on two realistic photochemical systems, thymine and azobenzene. The resulting models accurately reproduce energies and oscillator strengths for the ground- and low-lying excited states relevant to the photochemistry of these systems. We highlight the performance of the trained networks by studying critical molecular geometries, including conical intersections and excited state minima. By construction, the proposed framework also recovers the emergence of Berry phase accumulation around conical intersections. By pairing key mathematical structure from quantum chemistry with the representation learning power of transformers, the presented architecture offers a qualitatively new path toward fast and accurate ground- and excited-state simulations.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a transformer-based neural network architecture that learns a latent, implicit basis representation of the electronic-state Hamiltonian, enabling unified modeling of ground and excited electronic states, conical intersections, and non-adiabatic couplings for arbitrary molecular systems. The framework is demonstrated on thymine and azobenzene photochemical systems, accurately reproducing energies and oscillator strengths, and naturally recovers Berry phase accumulation around conical intersections.
AI.motivation: Traditional quantum chemistry simulations of excited states and non-adiabatic dynamics are computationally expensive, limiting their application to realistic photochemical systems. There is a need for a fast, accurate, and general framework that can model multiple electronic states and critical features like conical intersections and non-adiabatic couplings in a unified manner.
AI.method: The authors propose a neural network architecture that indirectly learns a latent, implicit basis representation of the electronic-state Hamiltonian. This approach provides a unified treatment of multiple electronic states, conical intersections, and non-adiabatic couplings, and can be extended to learn consistent latent representations of additional operators such as transition dipole moments. The model leverages transformer-based representation learning paired with quantum chemistry mathematical structure.
AI.result: Networks were trained and evaluated on two realistic photochemical systems—thymine and azobenzene. The models accurately reproduce energies and oscillator strengths for ground- and low-lying excited states relevant to photochemistry. The framework correctly handles critical molecular geometries including conical intersections and excited state minima, and by construction recovers Berry phase accumulation around conical intersections.
AI.conclusion: By combining key mathematical structure from quantum chemistry with the representation learning capabilities of transformers, the proposed architecture offers a qualitatively new path toward fast and accurate ground- and excited-state simulations of molecular systems, with potential for photochemical and non-adiabatic dynamics applications.

title: Symmetry-selective nonrelativistic spin splitting in antiferromagnets driven by coherent phonons
summary: Nonrelativistic spin splitting (NRSS) in antiferromagnets (AFMs) enables magnetization-free spin polarization for ultrafast spintronics. Here, we demonstrate that coherent phonons can dynamically induce and control NRSS in collinear AFMs. Excitation of $Γ$-point infrared-active phonons lifts the spin degeneracy of the ground state, while the residual sublattice-connecting symmetries determine the momentum-space form of the induced splitting. Because the relevant infrared modes couple to orthogonal in-plane light polarizations, distinct spin-split phases can be selectively activated by the polarization of the driving field. Using first-principles calculations for MnPS$_3$, we show that a mode that breaks all sublattice-connecting symmetries induces an $s$-wave spin-split state with $Δ(Γ)\neq0$, whereas a symmetry-distinct mode that preserves a sublattice-connecting mirror symmetry generates a $d$-wave altermagnetic state with $Δ(Γ)=0$. In both cases, the spin splitting grows linearly with the phonon amplitude and reverses the induced spin polarization when the displacement is reversed. Our results establish coherent lattice driving as a direct, polarization- and mode-selective route to dynamically induce distinct NRSS phases in AFMs.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that coherent phonons can dynamically induce and control nonrelativistic spin splitting (NRSS) in collinear antiferromagnets, achieving polarization- and mode-selective control over distinct spin-split phases (s-wave spin-split and d-wave altermagnetic states) through infrared-active phonon excitation.
AI.motivation: NRSS in antiferromagnets offers magnetization-free spin polarization for ultrafast spintronics. However, a direct and controllable route to dynamically induce distinct NRSS phases in AFMs remains an open challenge, motivating exploration of coherent lattice driving as a control mechanism.
AI.method: The authors use symmetry analysis combined with first-principles density functional theory calculations on MnPS3 to show that exciting Γ-point infrared-active phonons lifts ground-state spin degeneracy. They analyze how residual sublattice-connecting symmetries dictate the momentum-space form of the induced splitting and exploit the coupling of distinct IR modes to orthogonal in-plane light polarizations for selective activation.
AI.result: A mode breaking all sublattice-connecting symmetries induces an s-wave spin-split state with Δ(Γ)≠0, while a symmetry-distinct mode preserving a sublattice-connecting mirror symmetry produces a d-wave altermagnetic state with Δ(Γ)=0. Spin splitting scales linearly with phonon amplitude, and reversing the displacement reverses the induced spin polarization.
AI.conclusion: Coherent lattice driving provides a direct, polarization- and mode-selective pathway to dynamically induce distinct NRSS phases in antiferromagnets, establishing a new mechanism for all-optical, magnetization-free spin manipulation.

title: Tuning Boron-Vacancy Qubit Coherence through Layer Number in hBN
summary:
The negatively charged boron vacancy ($\VB$) in hexagonal boron nitride (\hBN{}) was the first optically addressable spin qubit identified inside a van der Waals crystal, allowing atomically defined placement relative to a target. Its coherence in bulk \hBN{} is limited by the boron nuclei of the layers flanking the defect plane, which a thin flake removes. Here, we use a generalized cluster-correlation expansion with an extended central-spin block to calculate the Hahn-echo coherence time of $\VB$ in h$^{11}$B$^{15}$N as a function of layer number. Our results show that $T_2$ rises from $199
s$ in the bulk limit to $653
s$ in a monolayer, a factor of $3.3$ that is already saturated at three layers and that a sublattice decomposition attributes entirely to boron. The enhancement is confined to low field, is insensitive to stacking registry and twist angle, and requires alignment to within about two degrees, an onset we reproduce with no free parameters. Under dynamical decoupling, a $1/e$ threshold returns $206
s$ for every thickness, but this is a zero of the first-shell modulation rather than a decay: measured without a threshold, the layer contrast survives and reaches a factor of $170$. Layer number thus emerges as a design parameter for $\VB$-based sensing.

AI.tldr: Researchers calculate the Hahn-echo coherence time ($T_2$) of the boron vacancy ($V_B$) qubit in h$^{11}$B$^{15}$N as a function of layer number using a generalized cluster-correlation expansion. $T_2$ increases from 199 ns (bulk) to 653 ns (monolayer)—a 3.3-fold enhancement saturated at three layers—attributed entirely to boron via sublattice decomposition. The enhancement is confined to low field, insensitive to stacking/twist, but requires alignment within ~2 degrees. Dynamical-decoupling contrast survives at a factor of 170 when measured without a 1/e threshold.
AI.motivation: To understand how layer number (flake thickness) affects the coherence time of the boron vacancy spin qubit in hexagonal boron nitride, given that bulk coherence is limited by boron nuclei in flanking layers and thin flakes can remove this decoherence source.
AI.method: A generalized cluster-correlation expansion (CCE) with an extended central-spin block is used to compute Hahn-echo $T_2$ times for $V_B$ in h$^{11}$B$^{15}$N as a function of layer number, combined with sublattice decomposition analysis.
AI.result: $T_2$ rises from 199 ns in bulk to 653 ns in a monolayer (3.3x enhancement), saturated by three layers. The enhancement is entirely boron-mediated, confined to low magnetic field, insensitive to stacking registry and twist angle, requires field alignment within ~2 degrees (reproduced with no free parameters), and under dynamical decoupling the layer contrast reaches a factor of 170 when no 1/e threshold is applied.
AI.conclusion: Layer number emerges as a design parameter for $V_B$-based quantum sensing, since thickness directly tunes the coherence time through the removal of flanking-layer boron nuclear spins.

title: A monolithic segmented 3D ion trap fabricated from fused silica by selective laser-induced etching
summary: We present the design, fabrication, and characterization of a monolithic, segmented, three-dimensional linear Paul ion trap for quantum science applications. The trap is fabricated from a single fused-silica block using selective laser-induced etching (SLE) and is subsequently metallized, forming electrodes isolated by self-shadowing trench structures without the need for layer alignment or external shadow masks. The segmented electrodes allow for shaping of the axial potential, enabling the creation of anharmonic potential wells, such as those required for equidistant ion strings. In addition, they enable shuttling and splitting of ion chains. We discuss key design choices and SLE-imposed constraints on achievable feature sizes, and evaluate electron-beam evaporation and magnetron sputtering as metallization approaches. Across two independent experimental setups, we demonstrate stable trapping and control of linear chains of up to 33 $^{40}$Ca$^+$ ions, including approximately equally spaced configurations. The measured secular frequencies in both traps agree with boundary-element simulations at the percent level, with residual deviations attributed to stray electric fields in the presence of anharmonic axial potentials, rather than fabrication imperfections. We measure axial micromotion field strengths on the order of 100 V/m along the trap axis, in approximate agreement with simulations. For radial mode frequencies near 2 MHz and an ion-electrode distance of 300 um, we measure heating rates of the order of 10 quanta/s in all but one motional mode, which is elevated by a technical noise source. The presented trap design is thus suitable for a wide range of quantum science applications and demonstrates the viability of SLE for the fabrication of finely segmented, monolithic, three-dimensional ion traps.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a monolithic, segmented, three-dimensional linear Paul ion trap fabricated from fused silica via selective laser-induced etching (SLE) and metallized without alignment masks. It demonstrates stable trapping of up to 33 40Ca+ ions, with secular frequencies matching simulations at the percent level, low micromotion fields, and heating rates ~10 quanta/s near 2 MHz, validating SLE for fine monolithic trap fabrication.
AI.motivation: To develop a scalable, monolithic ion trap fabrication method that avoids complex layer alignment and shadow-mask requirements, while providing segmented electrodes for shaping axial potentials—needed for anharmonic wells, equidistant ion strings, shuttling, and splitting—for quantum science applications.
AI.method: A single fused-silica block is micromachined using selective laser-induced etching (SLE), followed by metallization to form segmented electrodes isolated by self-shadowing trenches. Two metallization approaches—electron-beam evaporation and magnetron sputtering—are evaluated. Key design choices and SLE-imposed feature-size constraints are discussed, and trap performance is validated via boundary-element simulations and experiments in two independent setups.
AI.result: Stable trapping and control of linear chains of up to 33 40Ca+ ions with approximately equal spacing was demonstrated in two independent setups. Measured secular frequencies agree with boundary-element simulations at the percent level; residual deviations are attributed to stray electric fields under anharmonic axial potentials. Axial micromotion fields (~100 V/m) matched simulations. Heating rates near 2 MHz radial modes were ~10 quanta/s in all but one mode (elevated by technical noise).
AI.conclusion: The SLE-based monolithic trap design is suitable for a broad range of quantum science applications, demonstrating that selective laser-induced etching is a viable route for fabricating finely segmented, monolithic, three-dimensional ion traps without alignment-critical processing steps.

title: Nonequilibrium corrections to conserved Ising criticality in scalar active matter: Ward identities, spectrum, and long crossovers
summary: Active scalar field theories break detailed balance in two physically distinct ways: through a field-dependent noise-to-mobility ratio $Θ(φ)=D(φ)/M(φ)$, and through the gradient activity of Active Model~B+. We classify the resulting perturbations of the conserved Wilson-Fisher fixed point in three dimensions. Working from the Martin-Siggia-Rose-Janssen-De~Dominicis (MSRJD) action, a functional renormalization-group (FRG) calculation shows that the transport sector has a block-triangular stability matrix whose leading odd mode has $y_{Θ_1}=-Δ_φ$, while quotienting the gradient sector by its detailed-balance-preserving tangent leaves a chemical and a current-like mode. Two smooth regulators give $y_{Θ_1}\simeq-0.52$, $y_J\simeq-0.56$ and $y_{\rm ch}\simeq-0.89$. The translation Ward identity represents the current operator by a stress-tensor divergence modulo chemical gradients; conservation and causality then make the active stability matrix triangular to all loop orders, and an explicit two-loop calculation in $d=4-ε$ finds no additional contact counterterm. The two slowest modes are separated only by the Ising anomalous dimension, $y_J-y_{Θ_1}=-η$. This relation is a dimension count that holds provided neither operator acquires a further contact anomaly, a condition we establish within the present truncation for $\mathcal O_Θ$ and verify through two loops for $\mathcal O_J$; under it the $d=3$ reference Ising value gives $y_{Θ_1}\simeq-0.5181$ and $y_J\simeq-0.5544$. We derive the parity-resolved finite-size scaling of this near degeneracy, identify block observables that separate the two modes, and show that when the current amplitude dominates the crossover scale lies far beyond any accessible system size.

AI.tldr: The paper classifies perturbations of the conserved Wilson-Fisher fixed point in three dimensions arising from active scalar field theories that break detailed balance in two distinct ways: a field-dependent noise-to-mobility ratio Θ(φ) and gradient activity from Active Model B+. Using a functional renormalization-group (FRG) calculation from the MSRJD action, the authors find a block-triangular stability matrix with leading odd-mode exponent y_Θ1 ≈ -0.52, a current-like mode y_J ≈ -0.56, and a chemical mode y_ch ≈ -0.89. They establish that conservation and causality make the stability matrix triangular to all loop orders, derive the exact relation y_J - y_Θ1 = -η (separated only by the Ising anomalous dimension), and identify observables that can distinguish the near-degenerate modes in finite-size scaling.
AI.motivation: The goal is to understand and classify the distinct renormalization-group behaviors of perturbations that break detailed balance in active scalar field theories, specifically determining the universality classes and scaling exponents near the conserved Wilson-Fisher fixed point in d=3, where two different mechanisms of detailed-balance violation (noise-to-mobility ratio and gradient activity) can compete.
AI.method: The analysis is based on the Martin-Siggia-Rose-Janssen-De Dominicis (MSRJD) action formulation combined with a functional renormalization-group (FRG) calculation. The stability matrix is analyzed near the conserved Wilson-Fisher fixed point, using two smooth regulators to compute critical exponents. The translation Ward identity relates the current operator to a stress-tensor divergence modulo chemical gradients, which combined with conservation and causality yields a block-triangular structure for the stability matrix valid to all loop orders. An explicit two-loop calculation in d=4-ε checks for contact counterterms.
AI.result: The transport sector exhibits a block-triangular stability matrix with leading odd mode exponent y_Θ1 = -Δ_φ. Two smooth regulators yield y_Θ1 ≈ -0.52, y_J ≈ -0.56, and y_ch ≈ -0.89. The relation y_J - y_Θ1 = -η holds, meaning the two slowest modes are separated only by the Ising anomalous dimension. Reference Ising values in d=3 give y_Θ1 ≈ -0.5181 and y_J ≈ -0.5544. No additional contact counterterm is found at two loops in d=4-ε.
AI.conclusion: The near degeneracy of the two slowest active perturbations is controlled by an exact exponent relation tied to the Ising anomalous dimension, provided no further contact anomalies arise—a condition verified within the truncation for O_Θ and through two loops for O_J. The authors provide parity-resolved finite-size scaling predictions and construct block observables that separate the two modes, show that when the current amplitude dominates, the crossover scale exceeds any accessible system size.

title: Thermodynamic Electric Toroidal Dipole and Intrinsic Longitudinal Spin Transport
summary: Electric toroidal dipoles (ETDs) characterize ferroaxial order, yet their bulk definition in periodic crystals has remained elusive because conventional multipole operators involve the ill-defined position operator. Here we formulate a thermodynamic ETD by coupling a spatially varying electric field to the relativistic spin-induced electric polarization. The resulting expression is gauge invariant and provides a bulk order parameter for ferroaxial phases. We further establish a direct relation between the chemical-potential derivative of the ETD and the intrinsic longitudinal spin conductivity in insulating systems. To demonstrate the formulation, we construct a minimal ferroaxial extension of the Kane--Mele model. The ETD becomes finite exclusively in the ferroaxial phase and is strongly enhanced near a small band gap, accompanied by a sizable longitudinal spin current. Our results establish a thermodynamic theory of ETDs in crystalline solids and identify the longitudinal spin conductivity as a direct transport manifestation of ferroaxial order.

AI.tldr: This paper formulates a gauge-invariant thermodynamic order parameter for electric toroidal dipoles (ETDs) in periodic crystals by coupling a spatially varying electric field to relativistic spin-induced electric polarization, and establishes a connection between the chemical-potential derivative of the ETD and intrinsic longitudinal spin conductivity in insulators.
AI.motivation: Electric toroidal dipoles characterize ferroaxial order, but their bulk definition in periodic crystals has been elusive because conventional multipole operators involve the ill-defined position operator, which is not well-defined in periodic systems.
AI.method: The authors formulate a thermodynamic ETD by coupling a spatially varying electric field to relativistic spin-induced electric polarization, ensuring gauge invariance. They then derive a direct relationship between the chemical-potential derivative of this ETD and the intrinsic longitudinal spin conductivity in insulating systems, and demonstrate the formalism using a minimal ferroaxial extension of the Kane-Mele model.
AI.result: The ETD is finite exclusively in the ferroaxial phase and is strongly enhanced near a small band gap, accompanied by a sizable longitudinal spin current. This demonstrates the formulation works and identifies a clear transport signature of ferroaxial order.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a thermodynamic theory of ETDs in crystalline solids and identifies longitudinal spin conductivity as a direct transport manifestation of ferroaxial order.

title: Parameter inference from a non-stationary unknown process using statistical feature-based slow feature analysis
summary: Non-stationary phenomena are ubiquitous, with examples to be found in climatological measurements, brain activity, and the behavior of financial markets. Starting with a time series from a non-stationary process, a key challenge is to infer the time-varying parameters that underlie the non-stationarity in these systems, without requiring a generative model of the dynamics to be learned. This problem is referred to as Parameter Inference from a Non-stationary Unknown Process (PINUP). Here we introduce a PINUP method called feature-based Slow Feature Analysis (f -SFA) comprising the computation of time-series features across sliding windows, followed by dimension reduction using slow feature analysis (SFA). This allows us to detect slow variation in a potentially wide range of statistical properties of the measured dynamics on a timescale determined by the window length. Crucially, using a comprehensive time-series feature set avoids the subjectivity of feature selection, while the SFA slowness constraint overcomes the bias towards irrelevant correlated features seen with variance-based dimension reduction. The performance of f -SFA surpasses that of four benchmark PINUP methods across a diverse range of non-stationary chaotic processes, and we explore the impact of various parameters on performance, including observation noise, parameter timescales, parameter amplitudes, and unseen parameter values. Further, applying f -SFA to sleep polysomnography data, we show that it is able to infer a time-varying parameter underlying the non-stationary sleep recordings that closely tracks depth of sleep. To our knowledge, this work presents the first comparative study of PINUP methods, and we demonstrate that f -SFA is a simple, effective, and noise-robust approach for quantifying non-stationarity from time series, that can be applied in a range of fields.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces f-SFA, a method combining time-series feature extraction across sliding windows with slow feature analysis (SFA) for parameter inference from non-stationary unknown processes (PINUP). It outperforms four benchmark PINUP methods across diverse non-stationary chaotic processes, is robust to noise, and successfully tracks sleep depth from polysomnography data.
AI.motivation: Non-stationary phenomena are ubiquitous in fields like climatology, neuroscience, and finance. A key challenge is inferring time-varying parameters underlying non-stationarity without learning a generative model of the dynamics. Existing PINUP methods rely on subjective feature selection or variance-based dimension reduction, which can be biased toward irrelevant correlated features.
AI.method: f-SFA comprises two stages: (1) computation of a comprehensive set of time-series features across sliding windows, and (2) dimension reduction using slow feature analysis (SFA). The comprehensive feature set avoids subjectivity in feature selection, while the SFA slowness constraint overcomes bias toward irrelevant correlated features found in variance-based dimension reduction. The window length determines the timescale of detected slow variation in statistical properties.
AI.result: f-SFA surpasses four benchmark PINUP methods across a diverse range of non-stationary chaotic processes. The authors explore the impact of observation noise, parameter timescales, parameter amplitudes, and unseen parameter values on performance. Applied to sleep polysomnography data, f-SFA infers a time-varying parameter that closely tracks sleep depth.
AI.conclusion: This work presents the first comparative study of PINUP methods. f-SFA is a simple, effective, and noise-robust approach for quantifying non-stationarity from time series, with applicability across a range of fields.

title: RBMD 2.0: Random batch molecular dynamics package for large-scale simulations on multi-GPU architectures
summary: Large-scale molecular dynamics simulations of particle systems on multi-GPU architectures are often constrained by the computational and communication costs of nonbonded force evaluation. We present RBMD 2.0, a major new release of the random batch molecular dynamics package designed for cross-node multi-GPU simulations of large-scale systems. It combines the improved random batch Ewald method with three-dimensional domain decomposition and ghost-particle communication to accelerate multi-GPU nonbonded force evaluation, while the DTK CUDA framework facilitates portability across heterogeneous accelerator architectures. Numerical experiments on multiple benchmark systems demonstrate both the accuracy and efficiency of simulations with RBMD 2.0. For simulations involving up to hundreds of millions of particles across multiple accelerator devices, one achieves speedups ranging from severalfold to approximately two orders of magnitude in nonbonded force evaluation while exhibiting over $97.5\%$ weak-scaling behavior. These results demonstrate the promising nature of RBMD 2.0 as a computational engine for future exascale molecular dynamics simulations.

AI.tldr: RBMD 2.0 is a major release of the random batch molecular dynamics package for cross-node multi-GPU simulations, combining the improved random batch Ewald method with 3D domain decomposition and ghost-particle communication to accelerate nonbonded force evaluation. It achieves speedups of severalfold to ~100x in nonbonded force evaluation for systems with up to hundreds of millions of particles, exhibits over 97.5% weak-scaling efficiency, and is positioned as a computational engine for exascale MD simulations.
AI.motivation: Large-scale molecular dynamics simulations on multi-GPU architectures are constrained by the computational and communication costs of nonbonded force evaluation, limiting scalability to larger systems.
AI.method: RBMD 2.0 combines an improved random batch Ewald (RBE) method with three-dimensional domain decomposition and ghost-particle communication to accelerate multi-GPU nonbonded force evaluation, while using the DTK CUDA framework for portability across heterogeneous accelerator architectures.
AI.result: For simulations of up to hundreds of millions of particles across multiple accelerators, RBMD 2.0 achieves speedups ranging from severalfold to approximately two orders of magnitude in nonbonded force evaluation, with over 97.5% weak-scaling efficiency.
AI.conclusion: RBMD 2.0 demonstrates promising accuracy and efficiency as a computational engine for future exascale molecular dynamics simulations.

title: A Generalized Approach for Incorporating Geometry and Directionality into Coarse-Grained Machine-Learned Potentials
summary: Machine-learned interatomic potentials have enabled highly accurate atomistic simulations, but extending these capabilities to coarse-grained systems remains challenging due to the loss of geometric and orientational information during coarse-graining. In this work, we present a generalized framework for incorporating molecular geometry and directionality into coarse-grained machine-learned potentials through two complementary approaches: anisotropic density-based descriptors (AniSOAP) and symmetry-adapted equivariant message-passing neural networks (MACE-CG). Using Gay-Berne particles and coarse-grained representations of benzene, formamide, and water, we demonstrate that explicitly retaining molecular anisotropy substantially improves the prediction of energies, forces, and torques relative to isotropic representations. AniSOAP provides an effective linear baseline when molecular shape is well approximated by ellipsoidal symmetry, while symmetry-adapted MACE-CG enables the incorporation of arbitrary molecular point-group symmetries. For water, whose orientational degrees of freedom are poorly represented by ellipsoidal descriptors alone, symmetry-adapted rigid-body features improve energy, force, and torque prediction by resolving orientational degeneracies inherent to isotropic and moment-of-inertia-based representations. These results show that information loss in coarse-grained modeling is governed not only by mapping resolution but also by the symmetry and geometric information retained in the representation, providing a systematic route toward more expressive and transferable coarse-grained machine-learned potentials.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a generalized framework for incorporating molecular geometry and directionality into coarse-grained machine-learned potentials via two complementary approaches: AniSOAP (anisotropic density-based descriptors) and MACE-CG (symmetry-adapted equivariant message-passing neural networks). Using Gay-Berne particles and coarse-grained benzene, formamide, and water, the authors demonstrate that retaining molecular anisotropy significantly improves prediction of energies, forces, and torques compared to isotropic representations.
AI.motivation: Machine-learned interatomic potentials have enabled highly accurate atomistic simulations, but extending these capabilities to coarse-grained systems remains challenging due to the loss of geometric and orientational information during coarse-graining. The authors aim to address this information-loss problem systematically.
AI.method: The paper proposes two complementary frameworks: (1) AniSOAP, an anisotropic density-based descriptor approach that serves as a linear baseline, effective when molecular shape approximates ellipsoidal symmetry; and (2) MACE-CG, a symmetry-adapted equivariant message-passing neural network that can incorporate arbitrary molecular point-group symmetries. Both are tested on Gay-Berne particles and coarse-grained representations of benzene, formamide, and water.

AniSOAP works well for ellipsoidal systems, while MACE-CG handles arbitrary point-group symmetries. For water, symmetry-adapted rigid-body features resolve orientational degeneracies inherent in isotropic and moment-of-inertia-based representations, improving prediction accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Information loss in coarse-grained modeling is governed not only by mapping resolution but also by the symmetry and geometric information retained in the representation. This provides a systematic route toward more expressive and transferable coarse-grained machine-learned potentials.

title: Molecular spin qubits in a van der Waals bottle
summary: Advancing quantum information technologies requires qubits whose coherence can be precisely engineered. Among the qubit platforms in development, molecular spin qubits (MSQs) stand out for their atomic scale tunability and chemical specificity, making them powerful candidates for sensing, simulation, and information processing. However, integrating MSQs into solid-state architectures without degrading their coherence remains a central challenge. Here, we introduce van der Waals (vdW) confinement within two-dimensional materials as a strategy for stabilizing quantum states in MSQs by engineering their local electronic, vibrational, and symmetry environments. Using cobaltocene as a model system, we show that confinement within vdW SnS2 and CdPS3 single crystals reorganizes the single-ion energy landscape and slows spin-lattice relaxation by over two orders of magnitude relative to unconfined cobaltocene. The confined MSQs adopt deterministic orientations and self-assemble into ordered, atomically precise superlattices, establishing vdW confinement as a pathway for integrating MSQs into functional quantum devices.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces van der Waals (vdW) confinement within two-dimensional materials as a strategy to stabilize molecular spin qubits (MSQs). Using cobaltocene confined in vdW SnS2 and CdPS3 single crystals, the authors show that confinement reorganizes the single-ion energy landscape, slowing spin-lattice relaxation by over two orders of magnitude compared to unconfined cobaltocene. The confined MSQs self-assemble into ordered, atomically precise superlattices with deterministic orientations, establishing vdW confinement as a viable pathway for integrating MSQs into quantum devices.
AI.motivation: Molecular spin qubits offer atomic-scale tunability and chemical specificity, making them promising for quantum sensing, simulation, and information processing. However, a central challenge is integrating MSQs into solid-state architectures without degrading their coherence. This work aims to overcome this limitation by using vdW confinement to engineer the local electronic, vibrational, and symmetry environments of MSQs to preserve and enhance their quantum properties.
AI.method: The authors employ van der Waals confinement by intercalating/hosting cobaltocene within two-dimensional SnS2 and CdPS3 single crystals. This approach engineers the local electronic, vibrational, and symmetry environments of the MSQs. They compare the spin-lattice relaxation behavior and energy landscape of confined cobaltocene versus unconfined cobaltocene to assess the effects of confinement.
AI.result: Confinement within vdW SnS2 and CdPS3 single crystals reorganizes the single-ion energy landscape of cobaltocene and slows spin-lattice relaxation by more than two orders of magnitude compared to unconfined cobaltocene. Furthermore, the confined MSQs exhibit deterministic orientations and self-assemble into ordered, atomically precise superlattices.
AI.conclusion: vdW confinement within two-dimensional materials represents an effective strategy to stabilize molecular spin qubits and integrate them into functional solid-state quantum devices, offering a pathway to leverage the chemical tunability of MSQs while preserving their coherence.

title: Magnons in Metallic Altermagnetic $\text{KV}_2\text{Se}_2\text{O}$
summary: We investigate the spin excitation in altermagnetic vanadium oxyselenides, focusing on the metallic quasi-two-dimensional compound $\text{KV}_2\text{Se}_2\text{O}$. Using a fermionic Hamiltonian derived from ab initio calculations, we compute the transverse spin susceptibilities within the random phase approximation and extract the magnon dispersion relation. We show that the altermagnetic symmetry leads to characteristic degeneracies and directional splittings in both the electronic bands and the magnon spectra along high-symmetry paths of the Brillouin zone. The metallic $\text{KV}_2\text{Se}_2\text{O}$ exhibits finite magnon linewidths arising from the coupling to the particle-hole continuum. Furthermore, by fixing the magnitude of the wave vector and varying its in-plane direction, we uncover a pronounced angular dependence of the magnon energies and lifetimes, with complementary damping behavior between the two magnon branches. Upon including spin-orbit coupling, the system exhibits an out-of-plane easy c-axis anisotropy, which opens a magnon gap of approximately 6 meV at the $Γ$-point, possibly rendering the magnetic order stable at room temperature. Our results demonstrate that altermagnetism controls not only the dispersion but also the anisotropic decay of spin excitations, highlighting altermagnetic metals as promising platforms for directionally selective magnon transport.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates spin excitations in the metallic altermagnetic compound KV₂Se₂O, computing magnon dispersions via random phase approximation from an ab initio-derived fermionic Hamiltonian. Altermagnetic symmetry induces directional splittings in bands and magnons; finite linewidths arise from particle-hole coupling, showing pronounced angular dependence of magnon energies and lifetimes. Spin-orbit coupling opens a ~6 meV magnon gap at the Γ-point with out-of-plane easy-axis anisotropy, potentially stabilizing magnetic order at room temperature.
AI.motivation: To understand how altermagnetic symmetry influences spin excitations in metallic compounds, specifically whether altermagnetism controls not only magnon dispersion but also anisotropic decay of spin excitations—highlighting altermagnetic metals as platforms for directionally selective magnon transport.
AI.method: Derive a fermionic Hamiltonian from ab initio calculations, compute transverse spin susceptibilities within the random phase approximation, and extract the magnon dispersion relation for quasi-2D metallic KV₂Se₂O. Study linewidths from particle-hole continuum coupling, analyze angular dependence by fixing wave-vector magnitude while varying in-plane direction, and incorporate spin-orbit coupling.
AI.result: Altermagnetic symmetry produces characteristic degeneracies and directional splittings in electronic bands and magnon spectra. Metallic KV₂Se₂O shows finite magnon linewidths from particle-hole coupling with pronounced angular dependence of magnon energies and lifetimes, including complementary damping between the two magnon branches. Spin-orbit coupling induces out-of-plane easy c-axis anisotropy opening a ~6 meV magnon gap at Γ, potentially stabilizing magnetic order at room temperature.
AI.conclusion: Altermagnetism governs both the dispersion and the anisotropic decay of spin excitations in KV₂Se₂O, demonstrating that altermagnetic metals offer promising platforms for directionally selective magnon transport and potential room-temperature magnetic stability.

title: Effect of reactive targets on diffusive transport with intermittent restarts
summary: We study search processes in a complex environment using the strategy of stochastic resetting. A common occurrence in these environments is targets with finite reactivity. Stochastic resetting has emerged as a powerful mechanism for optimizing search processes by curtailing long, unproductive excursions inherent to diffusive dynamics. Most theoretical studies, however, assume perfectly absorbing targets -- an idealization that overlooks the finite reactivity commonly encountered in realistic chemical and biological systems. In this work, we investigate the interplay between stochastic resetting and finite-target reactivity in reaction - diffusion processes. Considering a one-dimensional system with multiple reactive targets, we demonstrated that the target reactivity modifies the optimization landscape. We uncover distinct regimes in which resetting enhances transport efficiency towards specific targets based on their chemical kinetics. As a consequence, the optimal resetting rate becomes intrinsically reactivity dependent. Our results identify target reactivity as a crucial control parameter governing stochastic transport and provide insights into reaction-diffusion processes in complex media.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how stochastic resetting interacts with finite target reactivity in reaction-diffusion processes. In a one-dimensional system with multiple reactive targets, the authors show that target reactivity alters the optimization landscape of resetting, creating distinct regimes where resetting enhances transport efficiency differently depending on chemical kinetics, making the optimal resetting rate inherently reactivity-dependent.
AI.motivation: Most theoretical studies of stochastic resetting assume perfectly absorbing targets, which is an idealization that overlooks the finite reactivity commonly found in realistic chemical and biological systems. Understanding how finite target reactivity modifies the resetting optimization landscape is necessary for realistic applications.
AI.method: The authors study a one-dimensional reaction-diffusion system with multiple reactive targets, analyzing the interplay between stochastic resetting and finite-target reactivity. They systematically examine how target reactivity reshapes the optimization landscape and identify regimes based on chemical kinetics.
AI.result: Target reactivity was shown to modify the optimization landscape of stochastic resetting. Distinct regimes were uncovered where resetting enhances transport efficiency toward specific targets depending on their chemical kinetics, and the optimal resetting rate was found to be intrinsically dependent on target reactivity.
AI.conclusion: Target reactivity is a crucial control parameter governing stochastic transport under resetting. The findings provide new insights into reaction-diffusion processes in complex media where finite reactivity is the norm rather than the exception.

title: Prominent Dimensional Effects on High-order Harmonic Generation in Strongly Correlated Electron Systems
summary: Dimensionality strongly affects elementary excitations in correlated quantum materials, yet its impact on extreme nonlinear optical responses remains largely unexplored. Here, we combine high-harmonic generation (HHG) experiments on quasi-one-dimensional SrCuO$_2$ and quasi-two-dimensional Pr$_2$CuO$_4$ with nonequilibrium simulations of Hubbard models. We find a pronounced dimensional contrast: SrCuO$_2$ exhibits a robust plateau-like high-harmonic spectrum with weak temperature dependence, whereas Pr$_2$CuO$_4$ shows a monotonic decrease in harmonic yield and strong thermal suppression, especially at higher harmonics. The simulations qualitatively reproduce these trends and identify dimensionality-dependent doublon--holon dephasing, governed by spin--charge coupling, as their microscopic origin. These results establish dimensionality and spin--charge coupling as key control parameters for extreme nonlinear optical responses in correlated insulators.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how dimensionality affects high-harmonic generation (HHG) in correlated quantum materials by comparing quasi-one-dimensional SrCuO2 and quasi-two-dimensional Pr2CuO4. Experiments combined with Hubbard model simulations reveal a pronounced dimensional contrast: the 1D material exhibits robust plateau-like harmonic spectra with weak temperature dependence, while the 2D material shows monotonic harmonic yield decrease and strong thermal suppression. The microscopic origin is identified as dimensionality-dependent doublon-holon dephasing governed by spin-charge coupling.
AI.motivation: While dimensionality is known to strongly affect elementary excitations in correlated quantum materials, its impact on extreme nonlinear optical responses such as high-harmonic generation remains largely unexplored. This gap motivates the systematic experimental and theoretical investigation of dimensionality's role in HHG from correlated insulators.
AI.method: The study combines HHG experiments on quasi-1D SrCuO2 and quasi-2D Pr2CuO4 cuprates with nonequilibrium simulations of Hubbard models to compare and interpret the nonlinear optical response across different dimensionalities. Temperature-dependent harmonic yield measurements are paired with theoretical modeling to extract microscopic mechanisms.
AI.result: A pronounced dimensional contrast is found: SrCuO2 shows a robust plateau-like high-harmonic spectrum with weak temperature dependence, whereas Pr2CuO4 displays a monotonic decrease in harmonic yield and strong thermal suppression, especially at higher harmonics. Simulations qualitatively reproduce these trends and attribute them to dimensionality-dependent doublon-holon dephasing controlled by spin-charge coupling.
AI.conclusion: Dimensionality and spin-charge coupling are established as key control parameters for extreme nonlinear optical responses in correlated insulators, providing new insight into how low-dimensional geometry governs HHG and related nonlinear phenomena in strongly correlated systems.

title: Multi-fidelity Monte Carlo estimation of floor response spectra under combined seismic and structural parameter uncertainties
summary: Floor response spectra (FRS) are essential tools for the design of non-structural elements (such as equipment or components). Given the various physical phenomena influencing FRS, high-fidelity (HF) mechanical models of the primary structure may be required to estimate them. Since numerical simulations based on such models are generally computationally expensive, this paper proposes using a multi-fidelity Monte Carlo (MFMC) approach for the efficient estimation of FRS. The method relies on using observations from a fast low-fidelity (LF) model as control variables. If the absolute value of the correlation between LF and HF samples is close to 1, this approach reduces both variance and estimation error compared to a standard Monte Carlo estimate based solely on HF data samples. Through a case study involving the reactor building of the Kashiwazaki-Kariwa nuclear power plant, we demonstrate the suitability of this method for FRS estimation. It effectively reduces variance and estimation error, even when using a LF model as simple as a single-degree-of-freedom system. We also show that the method accounts for modeling uncertainties while maintaining comparable performance. Its ease of use makes it a valuable tool for practitioners.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a multi-fidelity Monte Carlo (MFMC) approach for efficient estimation of floor response spectra (FRS) in structural engineering, using observations from a fast low-fidelity (LF) model as control variables to reduce variance and estimation error compared to standard Monte Carlo methods based solely on high-fidelity (HF) data.
AI.motivation: Floor response spectra are essential for designing non-structural elements, but high-fidelity mechanical models of primary structures used to estimate them are computationally expensive to run in numerical simulations, creating a need for more efficient estimation methods.
AI.method: The paper employs a multi-fidelity Monte Carlo (MFMC) approach where a fast low-fidelity model is used as control variables alongside the high-fidelity model. The method exploits correlation between LF and HF samples—when the absolute correlation is near 1, the approach reduces both variance and estimation error relative to standard Monte Carlo based only on HF samples.
AI.result: Through a case study on the reactor building of the Kashiwazaki-Kariwa nuclear power plant, the method demonstrated suitability for FRS estimation, effectively reducing variance and estimation error even when using a very simple LF model such as a single-degree-of-freedom system. The method also accounts for modeling uncertainties while maintaining comparable performance.
AI.conclusion: The MFMC approach is a valuable, easy-to-use tool for practitioners in FRS estimation, offering significant computational efficiency gains without sacrificing accuracy.

title: Learning Spectral-Like Mesh-Free Discretisations
summary: Meshfree methods such as smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) with kernel corrections, radial basis function-generated finite differences (RBF-FD), and the local anisotropic basis function method (LABFM) construct discrete differential operators by imposing polynomial consistency on a local stencil. For stencils containing more nodes than there are consistency constraints, the resulting linear system is underdetermined, and the remaining degrees of freedom are fixed implicitly by the choice of kernel, basis preconditioning, or a minimum-norm condition. Polynomial consistency constrains the operator only in the low-wavenumber limit, and no part of the construction selects for accuracy at the wavenumbers where fine-scale content resides. We introduce Spectral-like Neural Discretisation (SpeND), in which the choice of those degrees of freedom is cast as a learning problem: stencil weights are parametrised by a neural network conditioned on the local node geometry, trained to approximate the modal response of a spectral operator over the resolvable band. A hard-constrained projection layer maps the network output onto the affine subspace of consistent weights, so that polynomial consistency holds exactly by construction rather than as a penalty. Training is self-supervised and physics-agnostic, requiring no reference solutions; the objective minimises dispersion and dissipation error over a prescribed band-limited function space. Modal analysis on disordered two-dimensional node distributions shows that the learned fourth-order operator follows the exact response over a substantially wider band than either explicit LABFM at equal stencil size or fourth-order finite differences on a structured grid, whilst recovering the expected fourth-order convergence rate under refinement.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Spectral-like Neural Discretisation (SpeND), a method that uses a neural network to parametrize stencil weights in meshfree differential operators, trained self-supervisingly to match the modal response of spectral operators over a wide band while enforcing polynomial consistency exactly via a projection layer. It outperforms LABFM and structured-grid finite differences on disordered node distributions.
AI.motivation: Existing meshfree methods (SPH, RBF-FD, LABFM) impose polynomial consistency on local stencils, which constrains operators only in the low-wavenumber limit. When a stencil has more nodes than consistency constraints, the remaining degrees of freedom are chosen implicitly (by kernel choice, preconditioning, or minimum-norm), leaving room to improve accuracy at wavenumbers where fine-scale content actually resides.
AI.method: SpeND casts the selection of free degrees of freedom as a learning problem: a neural network, conditioned on local node geometry, parametrizes stencil weights. A hard-constrained projection layer enforces polynomial consistency exactly by projecting onto the affine subspace of consistent weights. Training is self-supervised and physics-agnostic, minimizing dispersion and dissipation error over a prescribed band-limited function space with no reference solutions required.
AI.result: Modal analysis on disordered two-dimensional node distributions shows the learned fourth-order operator tracks the exact spectral response over a substantially wider band than explicit LABFM at equal stencil size or fourth-order finite differences on structured grids, while recovering the expected fourth-order convergence rate under refinement.
AI.conclusion: SpeND demonstrates that learning-based selection of underdetermined degrees of freedom in meshfree discretization can significantly broaden the accurate resolvable band without sacrificing polynomial consistency or convergence order, offering a principled data-free alternative to heuristic choices in operator construction.

title: Biquaternion Algebra with Bilinear Multiplication: A General, Elegant, and Computationally Advantageous Framework for Relativistic Electronic Structure Calculations on CPUs and GPUs
summary: Quaternion algebra provides a natural representation of time-reversal-symmetric matrix structures in relativistic electronic-structure theory, whereas complementary time-reversal-antisymmetric structures extend this representation to complex quaternions, or biquaternions. Here, we explicitly exploit biquaternion algebra for fundamental objects, including operators, kinetically and magnetically balanced basis functions, and their expectation values, within a unified framework encompassing real, complex, and real quaternion subalgebras as special cases. To realize this framework computationally, we have developed HMATLIB, a biquaternion matrix library implemented within the ReSpect package for pure CPU and hybrid CPU/GPU execution. A key development is a bilinear algorithm for matrix-valued biquaternion multiplication that reduces the number of real matrix--matrix multiplications from 64 to 24 compared with the conventional component-wise approach, while the biquaternion representation effectively doubles the maximum accessible matrix dimension under the same 32-bit indexing constraint. Numerical benchmarks on modern CPU and GPU architectures demonstrate that the biquaternion formulation consistently outperforms its isomorphic complex-algebra counterpart. For the largest matrices reported, hybrid CPU/GPU execution accelerates bilinear matrix multiplication by approximately 5-8 times over pure CPU execution and matrix diagonalization by approximately 12 and 61 times relative to CPU oneAPI MKL and NVHPC OpenBLAS, respectively. These results establish biquaternion algebra as a general and computationally advantageous framework for modern relativistic electronic-structure calculations.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a biquaternion algebra framework for relativistic electronic-structure theory, implemented in a new library (HMATLIB within the ReSpect package) supporting pure CPU and hybrid CPU/GPU execution. A bilinear algorithm for biquaternion matrix multiplication reduces real matrix multiplications from 64 to 24, and benchmarks show consistent outperformance over complex-algebra counterparts, with hybrid CPU/GPU acceleration of 5-8x for multiplication and 12-61x for diagonalization on the largest matrices.
AI.motivation: To extend quaternion algebra—which naturally represents time-reversal-symmetric matrix structures in relativistic electronic-structure theory—to biquaternion (complex quaternion) algebra for complementary time-reversal-antisymmetric structures, and to provide a unified, computationally efficient framework for relativistic electronic-structure calculations.
AI.method: The authors explicitly exploit biquaternion algebra for fundamental objects (operators, kinetically/magnetically balanced basis functions, expectation values) within a unified framework covering real, complex, and real quaternion subalgebras as special cases. They developed HMATLIB, a biquaternion matrix library in the ReSpect package for CPU and hybrid CPU/GPU execution. A key contribution is a bilinear algorithm for matrix-valued biquaternion multiplication reducing real matrix-matrix multiplications from 64 to 24. The biquaternion representation doubles the maximum accessible matrix dimension under 32-bit indexing.
AI.result: Numerical benchmarks on modern CPU and GPU architectures show the biquaternion formulation consistently outperforms its isomorphic complex-algebra counterpart. For the largest matrices, hybrid CPU/GPU execution accelerates bilinear matrix multiplication by ~5-8x over pure CPU execution, and matrix diagonalization by ~12x and ~61x relative to CPU oneAPI MKL and NVHPC OpenBLAS, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Biquaternion algebra is established as a general and computationally advantageous framework for modern relativistic electronic-structure calculations, offering both representational unification and significant performance gains over conventional complex-algebra approaches on modern hardware.

title: Morphology and Dynamics of Self-interstitial Clusters in Irradiated Nickel
summary: Self-interstitial atom (SIA) clustering is a key early step in radiation damage evolution in face-centered cubic (FCC) metals, governing defect transport, recombination, and the long-term microstructural response of irradiated alloys. We combine molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and high-speed (>1000 frames/s) in situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to investigate the structure, energetics, and migration dynamics of SIA clusters in FCC Ni. MD simulations show that interstitials initially form disordered dumbbell clusters that evolve into either sessile Frank loops or glissile perfect (prismatic) loops; the latter progressively reorganize into compact ordered configurations with increasing mobility. Direct construction of both loop types over a wide size range, validated against MD-relaxed structures, shows that perfect loops are thermodynamically favored over Frank loops for cluster sizes N greater than or equal to 14, where N is the number of SIAs, with the energetic advantage increasing with cluster size. Nevertheless, substantial kinetic barriers allow Frank loops to persist as metastable defects. For perfect loops, diffusion coefficients computed over N = 16 to 400 reveal a nearly size-independent migration barrier of approximately 0.02 eV, while the diffusion prefactor decreases approximately as N^(-0.54). Trajectory analysis reveals a non-rigid, row-wise relay mechanism in which the number of participating atoms increases systematically with loop size, accounting for much of the observed prefactor scaling. Sub-millisecond in situ TEM observations reveal intermittent loop motion at velocities higher than previously observed but still several orders of magnitude below the intrinsic mobilities predicted by MD, indicating migration through a heterogeneous energy landscape of mobile and pinned states.

A detailed mechanistic picture bridging atomistic simulations and experimental observations is needed.
AI.method: The study employs two complementary approaches: (1) molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to model SIA cluster structure, energetics, and diffusion, including direct construction of Frank and perfect loops over a wide size range with validation against MD-relaxed structures; and (2) high-speed (>1000 frames/s) in situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to observe real-time loop migration dynamics at sub-millisecond timescales.

Perfect loop migration barriers are nearly size-independent (~0.02 eV) for N = 16-400, with the diffusion prefactor scaling as N^(-0.54), attributed to a row-wise relay mechanism where the number of participating atoms grows with loop size.
