The near-zero migration barrier of perfect loops makes them highly mobile in defect-free lattices, but experimental observations indicate that real microstructural environments impose pinning that dramatically reduces effective mobility.

title: Complete Topological Classification with P and T Symmetries: Revealing a Topological Invariant Invisible to K-Theory
summary: The K-theoretic framework provides a complete topological classification of the tenfold symmetry classes and has been generalized to incorporate crystalline symmetries. Here, we show that this classification is incomplete even in the elementary case of spinless systems possessing both P and T symmetries. We obtain the complete classification through a first-principles analysis of the topological classes of P- and T-symmetric bands, namely, by classifying the corresponding symmetric clutching data. We identify a topological invariant that is invisible from the K-theoretic perspective when the occupied states at each inversion-invariant momentum have uniformly positive or uniformly negative parity. In special cases, such as when all inversion-invariant momenta have uniformly positive parity, this invariant can be interpreted as the second Stiefel--Whitney class or the Euler number defined over an inversion fundamental domain, namely, half of the Brillouin zone. Our work not only reveals a new topological invariant that cannot be determined from the parity spectra at inversion-invariant momenta under P and T symmetries, but also demonstrates the existence of crystalline topological phases that are absent from the K-theoretic classification.

AI.tldr: The K-theoretic classification of topological bands, while complete for tenfold symmetry classes and extended to crystalline symmetries, is shown to be incomplete for spinless systems with both P (inversion) and T (time-reversal) symmetries. The authors provide a complete classification via symmetric clutching data and identify a new topological invariant invisible to K-theory when occupied states at inversion-invariant momenta have uniform parity. This invariant reduces to the second Stiefel–Whitney class or Euler number over half the Brillouin zone in special cases, revealing crystalline topological phases absent from the K-theoretic framework.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that the established K-theoretic topological classification, although seemingly complete for tenfold symmetry classes and generalized to crystalline symmetries, is actually incomplete even in the elementary case of spinless systems with both parity (P) and time-reversal (T) symmetries, and to uncover new topological invariants hidden from the K-theoretic perspective.
AI.method: The authors perform a first-principles topological classification of P- and T-symmetric bands by classifying the symmetric clutching data associated with these band structures, rather than relying solely on K-theoretic methods. This approach enables identification of topological invariants beyond those captured by K-theory.
AI.result: A new topological invariant is identified that is invisible from K-theory when the occupied states at every inversion-invariant momentum have uniformly positive or uniformly negative parity. In special cases—such as when all inversion-invariant momenta have uniformly positive parity—the invariant can be interpreted as the second Stiefel–Whitney class or the Euler number defined over half of the Brillouin zone. This demonstrates the existence of crystalline topological phases absent from the K-theoretic classification.
AI.conclusion: The K-theoretic classification is incomplete for spinless P- and T-symmetric systems, and the complete classification via symmetric clutching data reveals a new topological invariant that cannot be determined from parity spectra at inversion-invariant momenta, establishing the existence of crystalline topological phases beyond the K-theoretic framework.

title: Impedance in Periodically Driven Stochastic Systems
summary: We study the time-dependent currents arising in periodically driven stochastic systems. In the linear regime of small driving, a closed expression is obtained for the impedance/admittance associated with these currents. This expression leads directly to an interpretation in terms of an equivalent electrical circuit. For a stochastic system with $N$ states, the electrical circuit consists of precisely $N$ parallel branches, with each branch comprising a resistor and a capacitor in series. The low- and high-frequency limits of these currents are calculated, and the results are generalized to more general current expressions. We demonstrate our findings across several archetypal settings, illustrating the potential to detect specific broken symmetries or the graph topology associated with the stochastic process.

AI.tldr: This paper derives closed-form expressions for the impedance/admittance of time-dependent currents in periodically driven stochastic systems in the linear regime, revealing an equivalent electrical circuit interpretation with N parallel resistor-capacitor branches for an N-state system.
AI.motivation: To understand and characterize time-dependent currents in periodically driven stochastic systems through an equivalent circuit analogy, providing a framework to detect broken symmetries and graph topology.
AI.method: Analytical derivation of impedance expressions for stochastic currents in the linear response regime, analysis of low- and high-frequency limits, generalization to broader current definitions, and demonstration on archetypal stochastic systems.
AI.result: Closed-form impedance/admittance expressions yielding an equivalent electrical circuit with exactly N parallel resistor-capacitor series branches; validated across several archetypal settings showing sensitivity to broken symmetries and graph topology.
AI.conclusion: The equivalent circuit representation provides a powerful interpretive tool linking periodically driven stochastic thermodynamics to electrical network theory, enabling detection of structural features of stochastic processes through current response measurements.

title: Disorder-driven competing magnetic interactions and glassy magnetic behavior in quaternary Heusler alloy FeRuMnGe
summary: In this combined experimental and theoretical study, we investigate the role of disorder in governing the magnetic ground state of the quaternary Heusler alloy FeRuMnGe. In the FeRuMnZ (Z = Ga, Si) series, chemical substitution modifies atomic ordering and electronic structure, resulting in distinct magnetic ground states. Motivated by this, we extend the series to FeRuMnGe. X-ray diffraction reveals B2-type antisite disorder, where Fe--Ru and Mn--Ge intermix. Theoretical calculations show that such disorder modifies exchange interactions, leading to competing ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic couplings, and drives the system from half-metallic to metallic. Magnetic measurements reveal competing interactions, giving rise to a cluster-glass state coexisting with long-range magnetic order. The absence of a thermodynamic signature at $T_f$, together with ac susceptibility and relaxation measurements, supports the presence of short-range magnetic interactions and a glassy magnetic state. The compound exhibits an enhanced magnetic response below $\sim 161$ K and a maximum magnetization of $\sim 1.64~μ_B$/f.u. at 5 T. Overall, this work establishes a direct correlation between antisite disorder, competing exchange interactions, and glassy magnetism in quaternary Heusler alloys. Combined experimental results and theoretical calculations reveal that disorder drives the system from an AFM-dominated state in FeRuMnSi to an FM-dominated state in FeRuMnGe, providing deeper insight into the role of the extent of disorder in governing the magnetic properties of QHAs.

AI.tldr: This combined experimental and theoretical study investigates the quaternary Heusler alloy FeRuMnGe, showing that B2-type antisite disorder (Fe-Ru and Mn-Ge intermixing) modifies exchange interactions, drives the system from half-metallic to metallic, and produces a cluster-glass state coexisting with long-range magnetic order. The disorder shifts the magnetic ground state from AFM-dominated (FeRuMnSi) to FM-dominated (FeRuMnGe).
AI.motivation: To understand how chemical substitution and resulting atomic disorder govern magnetic ground states in quaternary Heusler alloys, extending the FeRuMnZ (Z = Ga, Si) series to FeRuMnGe and establishing direct correlations between antisite disorder, competing exchange interactions, and glassy magnetism.
AI.method: Combined experimental and theoretical approach: X-ray diffraction for structural characterization revealing B2-type antisite disorder, theoretical calculations to examine effects of disorder on electronic structure and exchange interactions, magnetic measurements including ac susceptibility and relaxation studies to probe competing magnetic interactions.
AI.result: B2-type antisite disorder (Fe-Ru and Mn-Ge intermixing) modifies exchange interactions causing competing ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic couplings, transitioning the system from half-metallic to metallic. Magnetic measurements reveal competing interactions producing a cluster-glass state coexisting with long-range magnetic order, with enhanced magnetic response below ~161 K and maximum magnetization of ~1.64 μB/f.u. at 5 T. Disorder drives the system from AFM-dominated (FeRuMnSi) to FM-dominated (FeRuMnGe).
AI.conclusion: Antisite disorder is a key parameter controlling magnetic ground states in quaternary Heusler alloys, establishing a direct correlation between disorder extent, competing exchange interactions, and glassy magnetism. The study provides deeper insight into how the degree of disorder governs magnetic properties in QHAs.

title: A Wannier-first approach for extended chiral systems
summary: We present a real-space formulation of DFT for extended systems in which localized Wannier-like functions are constructed directly from localized Gaussian basis functions without explicitly computing canonical Bloch-like states during the self-consistent cycle. Building on the formalism of Pederson and Lin [Phys. Rev. B \textbf{35}, 2273 (1987)], a variational set of Wannier-like functions is generated self-consistently within a finite Wannier domain and used to construct the charge density, electrostatic potential, and per cell total energy of the extended system. The occupied space can be determined entirely from the Wannier-like functions. Electronic band structures can be recovered in a post-processing step by solving the full Hamiltonian in a Bloch-like basis constructed from Gaussian orbitals. A key feature of the method is that it can incorporate combined translation--rotation, or screw, symmetries, enabling efficient simulations of chiral and helical systems with finite twist angles at essentially the same computational cost as systems described by pure translational symmetry. The approach is validated through calculations on linear and twisted $\mathrm{{-}C{\equiv}C{-}}$ and $\mathrm{{-}Li{-}F{-}}$ chains, as well as graphene, where total energies and band structures show excellent agreement with reference periodic calculations. To illustrate the ability of the method to treat three-dimensional systems, it is further applied to AA graphite, in which carbon atoms in adjacent graphene layers are aligned directly above one another, as well as helically stacked AA graphite structures. The Wannier-first framework provides a practical route for treating extended systems with nontrivial translational, rotational, and screw symmetries, and provides a natural foundation for the implementation of orbital-dependent functionals such as the Perdew--Zunger self-interaction correction.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a real-space formulation of DFT for extended systems where Wannier-like functions are built directly from localized Gaussian basis functions without computing canonical Bloch states during the self-consistent cycle. The method supports combined translation-rotation (screw) symmetries, enabling efficient simulations of chiral and helical systems at computational costs similar to purely translational systems. Validation on linear and twisted carbon-carbon and lithium-fluoride chains, graphene, and AA graphite shows excellent agreement with reference periodic calculations.
AI.motivation: Traditional DFT for extended systems relies on Bloch states and translational symmetry, which fails or becomes inefficient for systems with more complex symmetries such as chiral or helical structures with finite twist angles. A real-space Wannier-based formulation avoids computing canonical Bloch states during the self-consistent cycle and naturally accommodates screw symmetries, enabling efficient treatment of such systems.
AI.method: Building on the Pederson-Lin formalism, a variational set of Wannier-like functions is generated self-consistently within a finite Wannier domain using localized Gaussian basis functions. These functions construct the charge density, electrostatic potential, and per-cell total energy. The occupied space is fully determined from the Wannier-like functions. Band structures are recovered in post-processing by solving the full Hamiltonian in a Bloch-like Gaussian basis. The method incorporates combined translation-rotation symmetries for helical/chiral systems.
AI.result: The method was validated on linear and twisted -C≡C- and -Li-F- chains, graphene, and AA graphite (including helically stacked variants). Total energies and band structures show excellent agreement with reference periodic calculations, demonstrating the framework's accuracy and its ability to treat 1D, 2D, and 3D systems with nontrivial symmetries.
AI.conclusion: The Wannier-first framework provides a practical route for treating extended systems with translational, rotational, and screw symmetries at computational costs comparable to purely periodic systems, and offers a natural foundation for implementing orbital-dependent functionals such as the Perdew-Zunger self-interaction correction.

title: Prototype-guided transfer of sparse literature knowledge for electrolyte additive discovery
summary: Electrolyte additive discovery remains challenging because experimentally validated molecules are sparse, whereas accessible chemical spaces are vast and largely unlabeled. This challenge is amplified in lithium-ion batteries, where additive performance arises from coupled interfacial reactions rather than a single molecular property. Here, we develop a prototype-guided molecular intelligence, ProtoMI, a literature-driven framework that learns transferable structural priors from reported electrolyte additives and uses them to prioritize candidates in unlabeled chemical space. For boron-containing additives, ProtoMI combines 126 literature-reported molecules with 179,977 unlabeled candidates. Graph contrastive learning identifies seven chemically interpretable prototypes from the reported additives, and prototype guided semi-supervised contrastive learning adapts these prototypes to the candidate space under source-target distribution mismatch. In retrospective temporal validation, ProtoMI achieves enrichment factors of 9.2-45.6 while screening less than 2% of the candidate space. A subsequent translation step identifies four commercially accessible candidates. One representative candidate, 4,4,5,5-Tetramethyl-2-[10-(1naphthyl)anthracen-9-yl]-1,3,2-dioxaborolane (TNDB), improves high-temperature LiFePO4||graphite cycling at 55 °C by 34.93% relative to the baseline electrolyte. An arsenal of characterizations and operando optical fiber Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy suggest that TNDB forms B-containing, F/P/O-modified inorganic interphases, suppresses solvent decomposition and reduces Fe deposition on graphite. This case study shows how sparse literature knowledge can guide experimentally efficient molecular discovery in data-scarce battery-additive spaces.

AI.tldr: ProtoMI is a literature-driven framework that uses graph contrastive learning and prototype-guided semi-supervised contrastive learning to discover boron-containing electrolyte additives for lithium-ion batteries. It screens only ~2% of 179,977 unlabeled candidates using knowledge from 126 literature-reported molecules, achieving enrichment factors of 9.2-45.6 and identifying TNDB, which improves high-temperature LiFePO4||graphite cycling by 34.93%.
AI.motivation: Electrolyte additive discovery is extremely challenging because experimentally validated molecules are sparse while chemical space is vast and unlabeled. This is especially difficult in lithium-ion batteries where additive performance arises from coupled interfacial reactions rather than a single molecular property, making conventional screening ineffective.
AI.method: ProtoMI combines 126 literature-reported boron-containing additives with 179,977 unlabeled candidates. It uses graph contrastive learning to identify seven chemically interpretable prototypes from reported additives, then applies prototype-guided semi-supervised contrastive learning to adapt these prototypes to the candidate space under source-target distribution mismatch. A translation step then identifies commercially accessible candidates.
AI.result: Retrospective temporal validation achieved enrichment factors of 9.2-45.6 while screening less than 2% of the candidate space. The framework identified TNDB, which improved high-temperature LiFePO4||graphite cycling at 55 °C by 34.93% relative to baseline. Characterization and operando optical fiber FTIR showed TNDB forms B-containing, F/P/O-modified inorganic interphases, suppresses solvent decomposition, and reduces Fe deposition on graphite.
AI.conclusion: This case study demonstrates that sparse literature knowledge can effectively guide experimentally efficient molecular discovery in data-scarce battery-additive spaces, offering a generalizable framework that addresses the fundamental scarcity of validated data in electrolyte additive research.

title: Machine Learning Local Potentials for Accelerated Electron-Phonon Interactions Calculations within the Projector Augmented-Wave Framework
summary: Electron-phonon interactions govern carrier dynamics, transport, and many optical and quantum phenomena in solids, but finite-displacement calculations within the projector augmented-wave (PAW) framework require up to 6N self-consistent supercell calculations for an N-atom system, making them costly for large, low-symmetry, and disordered materials. We introduce MLLocP, a machine learning strategy that learns the self-consistent local potential on real-space grids and supplies its displacement derivatives to the evaluation of all-electron PAW electron-phonon matrix elements. Analysis of the PAW decomposition identifies the local-potential contribution as a natural target for machine learning, while the remaining PAW quantities are retained within the established VASP/PHELEL framework. Using targeted grid-point sampling and feature-diversity selection for efficient model training, we validate MLLocP for elemental Cu, polar BAs, and chemically disordered Cu3Au. The learned potentials and their resulting displacement derivatives closely reproduce direct density functional theory calculations, yielding transport coefficients within approximately 3.5% for BAs mobility, 8% for Cu conductivity, and 11% for Cu3Au conductivity. For the 32-atom Cu3Au special quasirandom structure, using 40 sampled configurations reduces the number of self-consistent calculations by about fivefold relative to the 192 displaced structures required directly; using 20 or 10 configurations increases the acceleration to approximately 10- and 20-fold, with conductivity errors of 14.3% and 18.6%, respectively. MLLocP thus provides a scalable route to PAW electron-phonon calculations in complex materials while preserving the underlying all-electron formalism.

AI.tldr: MLLocP is a machine learning strategy that learns the self-consistent local potential on real-space grids within the projector augmented-wave (PAW) framework to accelerate electron-phonon calculations. It reduces the need for 6N self-consistent supercell calculations by learning local-potential displacement derivatives, validated on Cu, BAs, and Cu3Au with transport coefficients within ~3.5-11% of direct DFT and up to ~20-fold computational acceleration.
AI.motivation: Finite-displacement electron-phonon calculations within the PAW framework require up to 6N self-consistent supercell calculations for an N-atom system, making them prohibitively expensive for large, low-symmetry, and disordered materials.
AI.method: The authors introduce MLLocP, which uses machine learning to learn the self-consistent local potential on real-space grids and supply its displacement derivatives for evaluating all-electron PAW electron-phonon matrix elements. The local-potential contribution is identified via PAW decomposition analysis as the natural ML target, while other PAW quantities are retained within the VASP/PHELEL framework. Targeted grid-point sampling and feature-diversity selection are employed for efficient model training.
AI.result: MLLocP reproduces direct DFT results closely: transport coefficients within ~3.5% for BAs mobility, 8% for Cu conductivity, and 11% for Cu3Au conductivity. For the 32-atom Cu3Au SQS, 40 sampled configurations reduce self-consistent calculations ~5-fold vs. 192 displaced structures; using 20 or 10 configurations achieves ~10-fold and ~20-fold acceleration with conductivity errors of 14.3% and 18.6%, respectively.
AI.conclusion: MLLocP provides a scalable route to PAW electron-phonon calculations in complex materials while preserving the underlying all-electron formalism, enabling study of large, low-symmetry, and disordered systems that were previously computationally intractable.

title: Persistence and emergence of quantum defects through pressure-induced phase changes
summary: Extreme pressures can transform materials and their properties, but probing these in-situ is made challenging by the small sample volumes and access requirements demanded by diamond anvil cells. Quantum defects offer a route to local measurements under such conditions, yet their sensing performance can be dictated by pressure-induced changes in their own host material. On the other hand, pressure may also be harnessed as a tool to engineer and stabilize new quantum defects with emergent functionalities. Here, we demonstrate both aspects within a unified platform based on optically active spin-pair defects in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). As robust quantum sensors under pressure, these spin-1/2 systems retain pressure-independent spin resonances up to 20 GPa while maintaining or even enhancing their optical emission, in stark contrast to the spin-1 boron-vacancy centre in the same material. Simultaneously, we show that compression acts as a means of quantum defect engineering: the starting hBN undergoes an irreversible transformation into wurtzite boron nitride (wBN), during which the defect landscape is reconfigured. Spin-pair sensors are seen to persist across this structural transition, however, depending on the starting material we also observe new, highly fluorescent defects in the wBN phase. These results establish spin-pair defects in boron nitride as pressure-resilient quantum sensors while highlighting high pressure itself as a versatile pathway for creating and tuning quantum emitters.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that optically active spin-pair defects in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) function as pressure-resilient quantum sensors up to 20 GPa while also showing that high pressure can be used as a tool to engineer new quantum defects via an irreversible hBN-to-wurtzite boron nitride (wBN) structural transformation.
AI.motivation: Probing materials under extreme pressure in diamond anvil cells is challenging due to small sample volumes and limited access, motivating the need for local quantum sensors. Additionally, pressure-induced changes in host materials can affect sensor performance, while pressure itself may serve as a tool to create and engineer novel quantum defects with emerging functionalities.
AI.method: The authors use optically active spin-1/2 spin-pair defects in hexagonal boron nitride as quantum sensors and characterize their spin resonances and optical emission under pressures up to 20 GPa. They also perform compression experiments that drive an irreversible phase transformation from hBN to wurtzite boron nitride (wBN) to study defect reconfiguration and the emergence of new highly fluorescent defects.
AI.result: Spin-pair defects retain pressure-independent spin resonances up to 20 GPa while maintaining or even enhancing optical emission, in contrast to spin-1 boron-vacancy centers in the same material. Upon phase transformation to wBN, spin-pair sensors persist, and depending on starting material, new highly fluorescent defects appear in the wBN phase.
AI.conclusion: Spin-pair defects in boron nitride are established as pressure-resilient quantum sensors, and high pressure is demonstrated as a versatile pathway for creating and tuning quantum emitters.

title: Branching stochastic mechanics. II. Relative localization and collective poles from Bohm/Fisher feedback
summary: Paper I introduced branching stochastic mechanics (BSM) by lifting the Schrödinger-Nagasawa pair to reciprocal forward and backward branching fields. Their centered connected kernel $C_{\rm FB}=\mathbb E_ω[ψ_Fψ_B]$ carries the organized reciprocal sector, where $\mathbb E_ω$ denotes expectation over branching-noise realizations, with $ρ_{\rm BSM}=-C_{\rm FB}(x,x)$ on the anticorrelated branch. Here we develop the stochastic field theory of the Bohm/Fisher feedback that acts on this connected sector. Starting from the multiplicative branching covariance of BSM, a Martin-Siggia-Rose-Janssen-de~Dominicis (MSRJD) formulation and a causal two-loop two-particle-irreducible (2PI) closure are used to determine response and correlation functions self-consistently. The free connected theory exhibits secular growth and ultraviolet accumulation, whereas the dressed theory develops a finite relative screening length. A reduced numerical evolution shows bounded formation of this localized sector, and a self-similar Fisher construction defines the saturated information velocity $c_\star$. A Born-Oppenheimer separation then distinguishes internal relative organization from collective propagation. Restoring the complete frequency structure gives two fixed-$q$ pole families: a gapless difference branch and a gapped sum branch. The infrared velocity of the difference branch approaches $c_\star$ at saturation. The common cone and the projected sum-sector gap are then formulated as additional fixed-point matching conditions for the collective theory.

AI.tldr: This paper develops the stochastic field theory for Bohm/Fisher feedback acting on the connected reciprocal sector of branching stochastic mechanics (BSM). Using an MSRJD formulation and a causal two-loop 2PI closure, it determines response and correlation functions self-consistently, showing that the dressed theory develops a finite screening length while the free theory has secular growth. A self-similar Fisher construction defines a saturation velocity c*, and the full frequency structure yields gapless difference and gapped sum pole branches, with the infrared velocity reaching c* at saturation.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to understand the quantum-statistical content of the connected reciprocal sector in branching stochastic mechanics, specifically how Bohm/Fisher feedback organizes localized structure and defines propagation characteristics, going beyond the free theory's pathological secular growth.
AI.method: The authors lift the Schrödinger-Nagasawa pair to reciprocal branching fields, build the centered connected kernel CFB = Eω[ψFψB], construct an MSRJD path-integral formulation from the multiplicative branching covariance, and implement a causal two-loop 2PI closure to compute response and correlation functions. A reduced numerical evolution and a self-similar Fisher construction determine bounded sector formation and the saturation velocity c*, followed by a Born-Oppenheimer separation and pole analysis of the full frequency structure.
AI.result: The dressed connected theory exhibits finite relative screening length in contrast to the free theory's secular growth and UV accumulation. Bounded formation of the localized sector is shown numerically, and a self-similar Fisher construction yields the saturation velocity c*. Restoring full frequency structure reveals two pole families at fixed q: a gapless difference branch whose IR velocity approaches c* at saturation, and a gapped sum branch, with the common cone and sum-sector gap arising as fixed-point matching conditions.
AI.conclusion: The Bohm/Fisher feedback on the connected reciprocal sector of BSM yields a well-behaved dressed field theory with a finite screening length, coherent collective propagation at a saturated Fisher information velocity, and a two-branch pole structure separating internal relative dynamics from collective propagation—establishing fixed-point conditions constraint the joint theory.

title: EuIn2Sb2: epitaxially stabilized axion insulator candidate with strong spin-orbit coupling
summary: Eu triangular lattice layer compounds described by the general formula EuA2X2 have attracted growing attention due to a wide range of layered crystal structures and corresponding magnetic topological phases, arising from the coexistence of large Eu magnetic moments and energetically inverted A and X bands. Among the EuA2X2 family, EuIn2Sb2 has been predicted to host robust axion insulator and higher-order topological insulator states by stronger spin-orbit coupling but has not been experimentally realized, including the structural identification. Here we report the epitaxial stabilization of EuIn2Sb2 by adopting the molecular beam epitaxy technique. Structural characterization reveals that EuIn2Sb2 films are based on a unique In-on-In stacking, forming a new trilayer structure distinct from previously predicted structures in the EuA2X2 family. In addition to the in-plane antiferromagnetic ordering at TN=10.5K, the stronger spin-orbit coupling and enhanced In-In hybridization in EuIn2Sb2 make it an ideal candidate of axion insulator and higher-order topological insulator phases. These results establish EuIn2Sb2 as a new member of the EuA2X2 family and offer an advanced platform for exploring these magnetic topological phases.

AI.tldr: The paper reports the first epitaxial stabilization of EuIn2Sb2 thin films via molecular beam epitaxy, revealing a novel trilayer In-on-In stacking structure distinct from previously predicted EuA2X2 family structures. The material exhibits in-plane antiferromagnetic ordering at TN=10.5K and, due to stronger spin-orbit coupling and enhanced In-In hybridization, is identified as an ideal candidate for hosting axion insulator and higher-order topological insulator phases.
AI.motivation: EuA2X2 compounds are promising platforms for magnetic topological phases due to large Eu moments coexisting with inverted bands. EuIn2Sb2 was theoretically predicted to host robust axion insulator and higher-order topological insulator states yet had not been experimentally realized, motivating this work to achieve its synthesis and structural identification.
AI.method: Molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) was used to epitaxially stabilize EuIn2Sb2 thin films. Structural characterization was performed to identify the crystal stacking, and magnetic measurements were carried out to determine the magnetic ordering temperature and nature.
AI.result: EuIn2Sb2 films were successfully grown and found to adopt a unique In-on-In stacking configuration, forming a new trilayer structure not previously predicted for the EuA2X2 family. The films display in-plane antiferromagnetic ordering at TN=10.5K. The combination of stronger spin-orbit coupling and enhanced In-In hybridization positions EuIn2Sb2 as an ideal candidate for axion insulator and higher-order topological insulator phases.
AI.conclusion: The findings establish EuIn2Sb2 as a newly realized member of the EuA2X2 family and provide an advanced material platform for investigating coexisting magnetic order with axion insulator and higher-order topological insulator physics.

title: HiPoly: a hierarchical polymer-native AI framework for property prediction and generative design
summary: Polymeric materials are central to modern technologies, with applications ranging from energy to health and transportation. Although AI has made significant advances in materials discovery, the hierarchical structure of polymers across multiple length scales makes them inherently difficult to represent in a unified and physically meaningful way. Here we introduce HiPoly, a polymer-native AI framework that processes complete polymer descriptions through a three-level hierarchical graph architecture built on the G2RINS representation. HiPoly encodes stochastic inter-monomer connectivity, composition, and molecular weight directly within its architecture, using physically motivated design principles that mirror the multi-scale nature of polymeric systems. The framework establishes an end-to-end AI-driven workflow from experimental formulation data to property prediction, generative molecular design, and physics-based validation through molecular simulations, all unified by a single polymer representation. We demonstrate state-of-the-art prediction accuracy for thermophysical properties of multi-component polymer systems, with ablation studies confirming that each hierarchical design choice contributes independently to model performance. As an example, the generative design pathway is applied here to the discovery of sustainable alternatives to persistent fluorinated polymers, where it is possible to identify and independently validate PFAS-free candidates with target surface-energy properties. This work demonstrates how polymer-native AI can accelerate discovery by linking representation, prediction, and design across complex polymer chemistries.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces HiPoly, a polymer-native AI framework using a three-level hierarchical graph architecture (G2RINS representation) to process complete polymer descriptions, enabling property prediction, generative molecular design, and physics-based validation unified by a single representation. It demonstrates state-of-the-art thermophysical property prediction accuracy and successfully identifies PFAS-free sustainable polymer candidates via generative design.
AI.motivation: Polymers are central to modern technologies but their hierarchical multi-scale structure makes them difficult to represent in a unified, physically meaningful way for AI-driven discovery, unlike simpler materials.
AI.method: HiPoly builds a three-level hierarchical graph architecture on the G2RINS representation that encodes stochastic inter-monomer connectivity, composition, and molecular weight directly within the architecture. It establishes an end-to-end AI workflow from experimental formulation data to property prediction, generative molecular design, and physics-based validation through molecular simulations, all unified by a single polymer representation.
AI.result: The framework achieves state-of-the-art prediction accuracy for thermophysical properties of multi-component polymer systems, with ablation studies confirming each hierarchical design choice independently contributes to model performance. Generative design successfully identified PFAS-free candidates with target surface-energy properties for sustainable alternatives to persistent fluorinated polymers, validated through molecular simulations.
AI.conclusion: This work demonstrates that polymer-native AI can accelerate discovery by linking representation, prediction, and design across complex polymer chemistries, showing a unified approach is feasible despite the inherent hierarchical complexity of polymeric systems.

title: Machine-learning screening and first-principles lattice dynamics resolve the most stable structure of NaCa(BH$_4$)$_3$ from a data-driven candidate search
summary: Equimolar NaCa(BH$_4$)$_3$ offers a theoretical hydrogen capacity of 11.24 wt.% and a decomposition enthalpy expected to fall between those of NaBH$_4$ and Ca(BH$_4$)$_2$, but it has never been prepared and no crystal structure has been reported. Predictions for it have so far been built within the perovskite family that its heavier homologues adopt. Here that assumption is removed. Six candidate frameworks were assembled from three independent sources --- experimentally determined ABX$_3$ borohydrides, a distorted perovskite from data-driven structure prediction, and an unbiased search over a structural database in which all 2238 generated candidates were relaxed with none excluded --- and at fixed charge-neutral composition the cation arrangement of every framework was enumerated exhaustively, 420 decorations reducing to 118 symmetry-inequivalent configurations, screened with a machine-learning potential and settled from first principles. The most stable structure is not a perovskite. It is a monoclinic framework of space group Cm, reached only by the unrestricted search, at $-$4.185640 eV/atom, 7.67 meV/atom below the best framework available beforehand; two chemically unrelated donor prototypes converge on it to 0.076 meV/atom, and its ordered cation arrangement is the ground state of its own series. Its phonon spectrum carries no imaginary mode at any wavevector the supercell resolves exactly and its relaxed-ion elastic tensor is positive definite, whereas the orthorhombic perovskite candidate is unstable to $-$2.401 THz. That contrast supplies a physical reason for the reported failure to obtain this composition in perovskite form, and the simulated diffraction pattern reported here identifies the predicted framework by seven reflections that neither parent phase nor the competing framework produces.

AI.tldr: A computational study predicts the crystal structure of the previously unsynthesized ternary borohydride NaCa(BH4)3. An exhaustive, unconstrained search over 2238 generated candidates reveals that the most stable structure is not a perovskite (as previously assumed) but a monoclinic Cm framework lying 7.67 meV/atom below the best prior perovskite-based prediction. The predicted structure is dynamically and elastically stable, and its distinct seven-reflection diffraction signature enables experimental identification.
AI.motivation: NaCa(BH4)3 is a promising hydrogen-storage material with high theoretical hydrogen capacity (11.24 wt.%) and an intermediate decomposition enthalpy, yet it has never been synthesized. Previous structure predictions were constrained to the perovskite family adopted by heavier homologues, and this assumption may have been incorrect—potentially explaining the failure to obtain this composition experimentally.
AI.method: Six candidate frameworks were assembled from three independent sources: (1) experimentally determined ABX3 borohydrides, (2) a distorted perovskite from data-driven structure prediction, and (3) an unbiased search over a structural database. All 2238 generated candidates were relaxed with none excluded. At fixed charge-neutral composition, every framework's cation arrangement was exhaustively enumerated (420 decorations reducing to 118 symmetry-inequivalent configurations), screened with a machine-learning potential, and settled from first principles. Stability was verified via phonon calculations (no imaginary modes) and elastic tensor analysis.
AI.result: The most stable structure is a monoclinic Cm framework (not a perovskite) at -4.185640 eV/atom, 7.67 meV/atom lower than the best previously available framework. Two chemically unrelated donor prototypes converge to within 0.076 meV/atom. The ordered cation arrangement is the ground state of its series. The structure is dynamically stable (no imaginary phonon modes) with a positive-definite elastic tensor, whereas the orthorhombic perovskite candidate is dynamically unstable (-2.401 THz imaginary mode). Seven unique reflections in the simulated diffraction pattern distinguish this framework from parent and competing phases.
AI.conclusion: The perovskite assumption was the obstacle to predicting/obtaining NaCa(BH4)3. The genuine ground state is a monoclinic Cm framework found only by an unconstrained structure search, and its superior stability over the perovskite candidate provides a physical explanation for the experimental difficulty in obtaining the perovskite form. The predicted diffraction pattern offers a roadmap for experimental synthesis and validation.

title: In silico design of magnonic lasing in constricted waveguides
summary: Analogue black-hole systems have been proposed in various physical platforms, including magnetic materials, offering rich physics and promising applications such as wave lasing. However, their practical realization and characterization remain largely unexplored. Here, we present an in silico study of magnonic black-hole phenomena in constricted ferromagnetic waveguides driven by spin-polarized currents. Using micromagnetic simulations with a two-dimensional Poisson solver to obtain realistic current-density profiles, we demonstrate the formation of a double-hole cavity bounded by analogue event horizons, enabling resonant spin-wave amplification. We characterize the resonances as a function of magnetic and geometric parameters and identify the corresponding spin-wave modes. We further show that gradual tapers enhance transmission by suppressing spin-wave reflections, while interfacial Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction can mimic the current-induced Doppler shift, substantially reducing the critical current density required for applications and, consequently, Joule heating. Finally, we demonstrate a spin-wave laser in which thermally excited spin waves undergo selective amplification and coherent emission at well-defined resonance frequencies. These results provide design principles for magnonic analogues of gravitational systems and point toward their potential for advanced spintronic applications.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an in silico (micromagnetic simulation) study of magnonic black-hole phenomena in constricted ferromagnetic waveguides driven by spin-polarized currents. Using a two-dimensional Poisson solver for realistic current-density profiles, the authors demonstrate the formation of a double-hole cavity bounded by analogue event horizons enabling resonant spin-wave amplification. They characterize resonances as functions of magnetic and geometric parameters, show that gradual tapers suppress spin-wave reflections, and that interfacial Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction can mimic the current-induced Doppler shift to reduce critical current density and Joule heating. Finally, they demonstrate a spin-wave laser with selective amplification and coherent emission at resonance frequencies, providing design principles for magnonic analogues of gravitational systems.
AI.motivation: To explore and characterize the practical realization of magnonic black-hole analogues in constricted ferromagnetic waveguides, addressing the largely unexplored experimental realization of analogue black holes in magnetic platforms and enabling potential applications such as wave lasing.
AI.method: Micromagnetic simulations combined with a two-dimensional Poisson solver to obtain realistic current-density profiles in constricted ferromagnetic waveguides driven by spin-polarized currents, enabling study of analogue event horizons, resonance characterization, taper effects, and Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction contributions.
AI.result: Demonstrated formation of a double-hole cavity bounded by analogue event horizons with resonant spin-wave amplification; identified resonance modes as functions of magnetic and geometric parameters; showed gradual tapers suppress reflections and enhance transmission; showed DMI can mimic current-induced Doppler shift reducing critical current density and Joule heating; demonstrated a spin-wave laser with selective amplification and coherent emission at well-defined resonances.
AI.conclusion: The results establish design principles for magnonic analogues of gravitational black-hole systems and point toward their potential for advanced spintronic applications, bridging gravitational analogue physics with practical spintronics.

title: Memory-driven Topological Defects and Unconventional Long-Range Order
summary: We investigate many-body systems with time-delayed self-interactions mediated by a memory-feedback mechanism. We show that such temporal interactions generate non-equilibrium orders and unique topological defects absent in equilibrium-specifically, helical vortices wherein opposite vorticities propagate in reverse directions along domain walls. In one dimension, memory feedback stabilizes true long-range order against weak noise, thereby circumventing the Mermin-Wagner theorem and resulting in an unconventional finite-temperature phase transition with a dynamical exponent $z = 4$. Physical realizations of these memory-driven non-equilibrium systems using active mechatronic metamaterials has also been proposed. These results demonstrate engineered temporal interactions as a powerful paradigm for non-equilibrium many-body physics.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates many-body systems with time-delayed, memory-feedback self-interactions, showing they generate non-equilibrium phases, helical vortices with counter-propagating vorticities, and stable long-range order in 1D (bypassing Mermin-Wagner), with a dynamical exponent z=4 and proposed engineering via active mechatronic metamaterials.
AI.motivation: To explore whether engineered temporal (time-delayed, memory-based) interactions can serve as a powerful new paradigm for realizing non-equilibrium many-body physics, producing phases and topological defects that are forbidden or absent in equilibrium systems.
AI.method: The authors theoretically analyze many-body systems with memory-feedback time-delayed self-interactions. They investigate ordering, phase transitions, and topological defect structures in such systems, including one-dimensional cases where they study the effect of memory feedback on long-range order and noise robustness. They also propose concrete physical realizations using active mechatronic metamaterials.
AI.result: Memory-driven temporal interactions produce non-equilibrium orders and unique topological defects, specifically helical vortices where opposite vorticities propagate in reverse directions along domain walls. In 1D, memory feedback stabilizes true long-range order against weak noise, circumventing the Mermin-Wagner theorem, and yields an unconventional finite-temperature phase transition with dynamical exponent z=4. Physical implementations using active mechatronic metamaterials are proposed.
AI.conclusion: Engineered temporal interactions constitute a powerful paradigm for non-equilibrium many-body physics, enabling phases and ordering phenomena inaccessible in equilibrium systems.

title: Charge-Transfer Electronic Structure of NiX$_2$ (X = S, Se)
summary: We investigate the electronic structures of NiS$_2$ and NiSe$_2$ using density functional theory combined with dynamical mean-field theory (DFT+DMFT). A realistic electronic structure within DFT+DMFT was determined by optimizing the double-counting correction to reproduce experimental valence-band photoemission spectra. The validity of the present model is further confirmed by its successful description of the Ni 2$p$ core-level photoemission and Ni $L$-edge x-ray absorption spectra of NiS$_2$. Our results reveal a smaller charge-transfer energy than previously assumed, resulting in substantial ligand-to-Ni charge transfer and a reduced Ni local moment. We clarify how the relative position and interaction between the Ni upper Hubbard band and the antibonding chalcogen-dimer states shape the evolution of the low-energy electronic structure across the NiS$_{2-x}$Se$_x$ series.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates the electronic structures of NiS2 and NiSe2 using DFT+DMFT, optimizing the double-counting correction to reproduce experimental spectra. It finds a smaller charge-transfer energy than previously assumed, leading to substantial ligand-to-Ni charge transfer and a reduced Ni local moment, and clarifies how the Ni upper Hubbard band and chalcogen-dimer states shape the low-energy electronic structure across the NiS2-xSex series.
AI.motivation: To obtain a realistic electronic structure for NiS2 and NiSe2 via DFT+DMFT and to resolve discrepancies between previous theoretical assumptions and experimental observations, particularly regarding the charge-transfer energy and spectral features.
AI.method: Density functional theory combined with dynamical mean-field theory (DFT+DMFT), with the double-counting correction optimized to reproduce experimental valence-band photoemission spectra. The model is validated through comparison with Ni 2p core-level photoemission and Ni L-edge x-ray absorption spectra.
AI.result: A smaller charge-transfer energy than previously assumed is revealed, resulting in substantial ligand-to-Ni charge transfer and a reduced Ni local moment. The interplay between the Ni upper Hubbard band and the antibonding chalcogen-dimer states explains the evolution of the low-energy electronic structure across the NiS2-xSex series.
AI.conclusion: The revised DFT+DMFT model successfully reproduces experimental spectra, providing a more accurate description of the electronic structure and clarifying the mechanism governing the low-energy electronic properties across the NiS2-xSex solid solution.

title: Symmetry-enforced third-order nonlinear thermal Hall effects in altermagnets
summary: Thermal Hall effect (THE) is a powerful probe of material properties, even in insulators. Here we investigate the thermal response of altermagnets by developing a theory on Berry curvature driven nonlinear THE from both electrons and magnons. We identify symmetry conditions under which the third-order THE dominates while linear and second-order contributions vanish. Notably, d-wave and i-wave altermagnets with out-of-plane Neel order satisfy these conditions, whereas in-plane order yields a dominant linear THE. Using KV2Se2O (a d-wave altermagnetic metal) and MnF2 (an altermagnetic insulator) as concrete examples, we show nonzero third-order nonlinear THE from electrons and magnons, respectively, both exhibiting a pi-periodic dependence on the direction of temperature gradient. These symmetry-guaranteed Berry curvature phenomena provide a diagnostic for altermagnetism in candidate materials and enable determination of the Neel vector orientation.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a theory of Berry curvature-driven nonlinear thermal Hall effects (THE) in altermagnets from both electrons and magnons. It identifies symmetry conditions where third-order THE dominates while lower-order contributions vanish, demonstrated in KV2Se2O (d-wave altermagnetic metal) and MnF2 (altermagnetic insulator), both showing pi-periodic dependence on temperature gradient direction.
AI.motivation: To understand and diagnose altermagnetism—a newly identified magnetic phase—through thermal transport signatures. While THE is a established probe of material properties, the thermal response specific to altermagnets has not been systematically investigated.
AI.method: Develops a theoretical framework for Berry curvature-driven nonlinear THE in altermagnets, analyzing contributions from both electronic and magnonic carriers. Identifies symmetry conditions that enforce vanishing linear and second-order THE while allowing nonzero third-order THE, and applies these to concrete material examples.
AI.result: Shows that d-wave and i-wave altermagnets with out-of-plane Neel order satisfy conditions for dominant third-order nonlinear THE, while in-plane order gives dominant linear THE. KV2Se2O and MnF2 exhibit nonzero third-order nonlinear THE from electrons and magnons respectively, with pi-periodic angular dependence on temperature gradient direction.
AI.conclusion: These symmetry-guaranteed Berry curvature phenomena provide a diagnostic tool for identifying altermagnetism in candidate materials and determining Neel vector orientation.

title: Room-temperature local strain control of moiré excitons in MoS$_2$/WSe$_2$ heterobilayers
summary: Moiré superlattices in heterobilayers of atomically thin transition metal dichalcogenides provide a versatile platform for exploring quantum many-body physics as they can trap excitons, leading to the formation of quantized moiré exciton states. However, such moiré excitons have been predominantly studied at cryogenic temperatures, which severely limits their practical applications. Here, we demonstrate room-temperature activation and control of moiré excitons in MoS$_2$/WSe$_2$ heterobilayers using local strain engineering. Applying mechanical strain with a modified atomic force microscopy tip, we observe a series of resonances attributed to interlayer exciton states confined in the moiré potential. Power-dependent photoluminescence measurements elucidate the population dynamics of the moiré exciton states, while controlled local strain enables continuous tuning of their emission wavelength to the center of the second telecom window. We provide a theoretical model that captures all experimentally observed features, including the unconventional spectral shape of the moiré exciton emission. Our findings establish local tip-induced strain as a powerful tool for the on-demand manipulation of moiré excitons, paving the way for room-temperature quantum excitonic devices.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates room-temperature activation and control of moiré excitons in MoS₂/WSe₂ heterobilayers using local strain engineering with an atomic force microscopy tip, enabling continuous emission wavelength tuning into the second telecom window and supported by a theoretical model.
AI.motivation: Moiré excitons in transition metal dichalcogenide heterobilayers offer a platform for quantum many-body physics, but they have predominantly been studied only at cryogenic temperatures, severely limiting practical applications. The authors aim to overcome this temperature barrier to enable room-temperature quantum excitonic devices.
AI.method: The authors apply mechanical strain locally using a modified atomic force microscopy (AFM) tip to MoS₂/WSe₂ heterobilayers, activating moiré excitons at room temperature. They use power-dependent photoluminescence measurements to study population dynamics, and develop a theoretical model to capture the observed features including the unconventional spectral shape of moiré exciton emission.
AI.result: A series of resonances attributed to interlayer exciton states confined in the moiré potential were observed at room temperature under local strain. The controlled local strain enables continuous tuning of emission wavelength to the center of the second telecom window. A theoretical model successfully reproduces all experimentally observed features, including the unconventional spectral shape.
AI.conclusion: Local tip-induced strain is established as a powerful and versatile tool for on-demand manipulation of moiré excitons at room temperature, paving the way for practical room-temperature quantum excitonic devices.

title: Thermodynamic optimization of thermal landscapes and energy barriers in a Brownian heat engine
summary: Spatial temperature fields in Brownian heat engines are commonly prescribed \emph{a priori}, and the resulting transport and thermodynamic properties are then calculated. Here we formulate the complementary inverse-design problem: determining the temperature profile and barrier height that optimize a chosen thermodynamic objective. We consider an overdamped Brownian particle in a symmetric triangular periodic potential under a constant opposing load and derive the exact stationary current and probability density for an arbitrary bounded temperature field, $\Tc\le T(x)\le\Th$. In the quasistatic limit, the efficiency becomes an exact functional of two inverse-temperature integrals over the uphill and downhill branches. Its rigorous global maximum under the pointwise temperature bounds is $η_{\max}=1-\Tc/\Th$, attained uniquely, up to sets of measure zero, by the hot-uphill/cold-downhill piecewise-constant profile. At finite current, however, the optimization changes qualitatively because the current is determined jointly by the cycle affinity and a nonlocal transport resistance. We derive the exact functional gradient and the corresponding box-constrained optimality conditions, showing that the current- or power-maximizing profile generally differs from the quasistatic efficiency optimum. For any prescribed temperature field, the current-maximizing barrier satisfies an exact balance between the marginal gain in thermal rectification and the marginal increase in transport resistance, with the characteristic estimate $U_0^*\simeq T_{\rm act}$, where $T_{\rm act}^{-1}=(2/L)\int_0^{L/2}\dd x/T(x)$.

AI.tldr: This paper formulates and solves the inverse-design problem for Brownian heat engines: instead of prescribing a temperature profile and computing transport properties, it determines the temperature profile and barrier height that optimize a chosen thermodynamic objective. For an overdamped Brownian particle in a symmetric triangular periodic potential under an opposing load, the exact stationary current and density are derived. In the quasistatic limit, global efficiency maximization yields η_max = 1 - Tc/Th, achieved uniquely (up to measure zero) by the hot-uphill/cold-downhill piecewise-constant profile. At finite current, optimization changes qualitatively due to the joint role of cycle affinity and nonlocal transport resistance, and exact box-constrained optimality conditions are derived. The current-maximizing barrier satisfies an exact balance between thermal rectification gain and transport resistance cost, with U0* ≈ Tact.
AI.motivation: To address the complementary inverse-design problem in Brownian heat engines—determining the optimal temperature profile and barrier height for a desired thermodynamic objective—rather than the standard forward approach where temperature fields are prescribed a priori and resulting properties are merely computed.
AI.method: The authors consider an overdamped Brownian particle in a symmetric triangular periodic potential under constant opposing load. They derive exact stationary current and probability density for arbitrary bounded temperature fields. In the quasistatic limit, efficiency is expressed as an exact functional of two inverse-temperature integrals, enabling rigorous global maximization under pointwise bounds. At finite current, they derive the exact functional gradient and box-constrained optimality conditions, along with an estimate for the optimal barrier height.
AI.result: The quasistatic global maximum efficiency is η_max = 1 - Tc/Th, attained uniquely (up to measure zero sets) by the hot-uphill/cold-downhill piecewise-constant profile. At finite current the optimization changes qualitatively; current- or power-maximizing profiles differ from the quasistatic efficiency optimum. The current-maximizing barrier satisfies an exact gain-resistance balance condition, with characteristic estimate U0* ≈ Tact, where Tact⁻¹ = (2/L)∫₀^{L/2} dx/T(x).
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a complete theoretical framework for the inverse design of Brownian heat engines, revealing that quasistatic optimality (hot-uphill/cold-downhill, Carnot-like efficiency) does not persist at finite current, where a nontrivial trade-off between cycle affinity and transport resistance dictates the optimal design through exact variational conditions.

title: Direct observation of flat bands in near-magic-angle twisted bilayer CVD graphene
summary: Advances in chemical vapor deposition (CVD) growth have driven graphene crystal quality to unprecedented levels, yet it is still unknown whether this route can realize the fragile flat-band and correlated states of the magic-angle (MA) twisted bilayer graphene (TBG). Here, we report on the experimental observation by room-temperature nano-angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (nano-ARPES) of flat bands in a TBG sample close to the MA, assembled via a grow-and-stack protocol based on low-pressure CVD of graphene on copper. Our study indicates electronic bands fully comparable to those measured in exfoliation-based samples and determines the size of the largest near-MA domain to be compatible with electronic transport experiments, motivating further experiments on flat band physics in CVD-graphene.

AI.tldr: The authors report the first experimental observation of flat bands in nearly magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene assembled via CVD growth and stacking on copper, using room-temperature nano-ARPES. The electronic bands are fully comparable to exfoliation-based samples, and the near-MA domain size is compatible with transport experiments.
AI.motivation: While CVD-grown graphene has achieved very high crystal quality, it was unknown whether CVD-based samples could realize the fragile flat-band and correlated states characteristic of magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (TBG), which are essential for studying strongly correlated physics.
AI.method: The authors fabricated TBG samples close to the magic angle using a grow-and-stack protocol based on low-pressure CVD of graphene on copper. They characterized the electronic band structure using room-temperature nano-angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (nano-ARPES).
AI.result: The measurements demonstrate flat bands in the CVD-grown near-magic-angle TBG sample. The electronic bands are fully comparable to those measured in exfoliation-based samples, and the largest near-MA domain is large enough to support electronic transport experiments.
AI.conclusion: CVD-grown graphene can indeed realize flat-band physics comparable to exfoliated samples, motivating further transport experiments to explore correlated flat-band states in CVD-based magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene.

title: Survival in a partially reactive wedge
summary: We investigate the power-law decay of the survival probability of a Brownian particle diffusing in an infinite planar wedge whose two sides are partially reactive and described by Robin boundary conditions. We employ matched asymptotic analysis to relate the long-time asymptotics to a stationary harmonic Robin problem near the apex. This approach determines the persistence exponent for arbitrary opening angles and yields the prefactor explicitly for the family of wedges with $α=π/n$ ($n=1,2,\ldots$). A simple extension of the apex prefactor to arbitrary angles is conjectured and supported numerically. This asymptotic behavior describes the crossover to the well-known result for perfectly absorbing wedges. As immediate applications, we also deduce the long-time behavior of the probability density function of the boundary local time on wedge sides, as well as the probability density function of the associated first-crossing time.

AI.tldr: This paper derives the power-law decay of survival probability for a Brownian particle diffusing in an infinite planar wedge with partially reactive (Robin) boundaries, using matched asymptotic analysis to connect long-time behavior to a stationary harmonic Robin problem near the apex.
AI.motivation: To extend known results for perfectly absorbing wedges to partially reactive wedges described by Robin boundary conditions, determining the persistence exponent and prefactor for the survival probability decay.
AI.method: Matched asymptotic analysis relating long-time asymptotics to a stationary harmonic Robin problem near the wedge apex; explicit prefactor derivation for wedge angles alpha = pi/n; conjectured extension by simple extrapolation to arbitrary angles.
AI.result: Determines the persistence exponent for arbitrary opening angles and explicit prefactors for alpha = pi/n family. A conjectured prefactor formula for general angles is numerically supported. The result captures the crossover to the perfectly absorbing wedge limit.
AI.conclusion: The asymptotic results also enable derivation of long-time behavior for the boundary local time probability density and the first-crossing time distribution for Brownian motion in Robin wedges.

title: Rank-Selective Optical Tomography of Higher-Wave Altermagnetism
summary: Identifying the spatial rank of higher-wave altermagnetic order optically is challenging because local electric-dipole response does not uniquely resolve distinct continuum harmonics. We show that finite photon momentum turns one-photon spin-resolved absorption into a rank-selective tomography. For the planar $|m|=\ell$ sector of an even-parity $\ell$-wave component, a joint Fourier projection in polarization and momentum angle isolates $\mathcal T_\ell\proptoη_\ell q^{\ell-2}$, yielding the hierarchy $d:q^0$, $g:q^2$, and $i:q^4$; phase changes track rotations of the selected magnetic harmonic. A Ward-consistent finite-$q$ microscopic calculation reproduces these powers without imposing them. Although discrete crystal symmetry can generate lower-order local aliases, they are orthogonal to the selected momentum harmonic and cannot contaminate it below $q^{\ell-2}$. In MnTe, whose nonrelativistic parent order is three-dimensional $g$ wave while spin--orbit coupling lowers the exact relativistic spin-momentum-locking symmetry, first-principles calculations show that more than $99.9\%$ of the Fourier power of the Néel-projected $A$-region spin-energy contrast remains in the parent $g$-wave-derived $m=3$ harmonic. Structured near fields place the required momentum window within experimental reach.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that finite photon momentum enables rank-selective optical tomography of higher-wave altermagnetic order. A joint Fourier projection in polarization and momentum angle isolates the ℓ-th harmonic term proportional to q^(ℓ-2), yielding a hierarchy where d-, g-, and i-wave orders scale as q^0, q^2, and q^4 respectively. First-principles calculations on MnTe confirm >99.9% of Fourier power remains in the parent g-wave-derived m=3 harmonic.
AI.motivation: Identifying the spatial rank of higher-wave altermagnetic order through local optical response is fundamentally difficult because electric-dipole probes cannot uniquely distinguish different continuum harmonics of the magnetic order.
AI.method: The authors show that incorporating finite photon momentum into one-photon spin-resolved absorption measurements converts it into a rank-selective tomography. They use a joint Fourier projection in both polarization and momentum angle to isolate the ℓ-wave harmonic term, and validate this through a Ward-consistent finite-q microscopic calculation plus first-principles calculations on MnTe.
AI.result: The approach yields a hierarchical scaling: d-wave (q^0), g-wave (q^2), and i-wave (q^4) contributions. Lower-order crystal-symmetry-induced aliases are orthogonal to the selected momentum harmonic and cannot contaminate results below q^(ℓ-2). In MnTe, first-principles calculations show over 99.9% of the Fourier power of the Néel-projected A-region spin-energy contrast resides in the parent g-wave m=3 harmonic. Structured near fields make the required momentum window experimentally accessible.
AI.conclusion: Finite photon momentum combined with joint polarization-momentum Fourier analysis provides a robust rank-selective optical tomography for higher-wave altermagnetic order, with theoretical and ab initio validation establishing its practical applicability.

title: Optimal-work feedback on particles with activity --- gliding on active fluctuations using positional information
summary: We study the minimum-work feedback control of particles subject to active fluctuations. Considering an active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particle confined by a moving harmonic trap, we derive exact optimal protocols following an initial position measurement. Our results show that nonequilibrium correlations between position and active fluctuations allow work extraction from the activity based on positional information only, i.e., without directly measuring the active degree of freedom, which was the focus of earlier literature. We find that depending on the persistence time, activity can either facilitate or impede transport relative to passive systems. Surprisingly, unlike feedback schemes based on direct measurements of the active fluctuations, positional feedback remains energetically advantageous even in the limit of infinitely persistent activity. Our results provide design principles for information engines and optimal control strategies operating in active environments.

AI.tldr: This paper derives exact optimal minimum-work feedback control protocols for an active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particle in a moving harmonic trap following an initial position measurement. It demonstrates that position-only feedback enables work extraction from activity via nonequilibrium position-activity correlations, without direct measurement of the active degree of freedom, revealing activity-dependent transport and persistent energetic advantages even in the infinite-persistence limit.
AI.motivation: To understand and optimize information engines and feedback control in active (non-equilibrium) environments, where previous work focused on direct measurement of active fluctuations, leaving open the question of what can be achieved with positional information alone.
AI.method: The authors analytically solve the optimal control problem for an active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particle confined by a moving harmonic trap, deriving exact minimum-work feedback protocols conditioned on an initial position measurement.
AI.result: Position-based feedback alone allows work extraction from activity via nonequilibrium correlations. Activity can either enhance or hinder transport depending on persistence time, and positional feedback remains energetically superior to passive control even in the infinitely persistent activity limit, unlike direct-measurement feedback schemes.
AI.conclusion: Positional feedback provides design principles for information engines and optimal control strategies operating in active environments, extending work-extraction capabilities beyond direct measurement of hidden active degrees of freedom.

title: The Locality Cost of Fully Flat Hopf Insulators
summary: Hopf topology permits a strictly finite-range Hamiltonian with one exactly flat topological band. We prove, however, that extending flatness to the complete two-band spectrum necessarily sacrifices strict locality or the gap: any gapped, Hermitian, translationally invariant two-band Hamiltonian with strictly finite-range hopping and two exactly flat bands has vanishing Hopf invariant. Equivalently, within this two-band setting, a Hopf band admits no compactly supported, translation-covariant, orthonormal Wannier generator. For factorized one-flat-band Hopf parents, the unavoidable partner dispersion equals the Gram symbol of translated compact localized states and encodes their nonorthogonality. Full flattening converts this dispersion into exponentially decaying but infinitely supported hopping. Model-independent bounds provide a sufficient criterion for finite-range approximants to retain the Hopf phase. An explicit model yields the axial decay length $ξ_z/a=1/\ln 2$, parameter-free hopping tails, and residual bandwidths testable in circuit and photonic lattices. Hopf topology therefore does not prohibit a flat band but forces the locality--flatness cost to appear as either partner-band dispersion or nonlocal hopping.

AI.tldr: A strictly finite-range two-band Hamiltonian can host exactly one flat topological (Hopf) band, but cannot host two exactly flat bands unless it sacrifices strict locality or the gap—any gapped, Hermitian, translationally invariant, strictly finite-range two-band Hamiltonian with two exactly flat bands has vanishing Hopf invariant. The unavoidable partner-band dispersion encodes nonorthogonality of compact localized states; full flattening converts this dispersion into exponentially decaying, infinitely supported hopping. A sufficient criterion for finite-range approximants to preserve the Hopf phase is given, with an explicit model yielding a parameter-free axial decay length ξ_z/a = 1/ln2.
AI.motivation: To understand the fundamental constraints that Hopf topology places on flat-band Hamiltonians—specifically whether one can have exactly flat topological bands in a strictly finite-range, two-band setting, and what costs (dispersion or non-locality) the topology forces.
AI.method: The authors prove by contradiction/construction that gapped, Hermitian, translationally invariant two-band models with strictly finite-range hopping and two exactly flat bands must have vanishing Hopf invariant. They analyze one-flat-band Hopf "parents" using the Gram symbol of translated compact localized states, show their partner dispersion encodes nonorthogonality, and demonstrate that full flattening is only possible with exponentially decaying but infinite-range hopping. They derive model-independent bounds as a flattening criterion and construct an explicit model with ξ_z/a = 1/ln2.
AI.result: Hopf topology forbids simultaneous exact flatness of both bands in strictly finite-range two-band systems while preserving the Hopf invariant and the gap. The locality–flatness tension must manifest as either partner-band dispersion (in finite-range models) or nonlocal (exponentially decaying but infinite-support) hopping (in fully flat models). A concrete model gives parameter-free exponential hopping tails and calculable residual bandwidths suitable for circuit/photonic lattice experiments.
AI.conclusion: Hopf topology does not prohibit a flat band per se, but imposes a strict cost: either the partner band must disperse (keeping hopping finite-range) or the hopping must become nonlocal (keeping both bands flat). This establishes a precise locality–flatness tradeoff dictated by Hopf topology in two-band systems.

title: Direct Observation of the Zigzag Edge States of a Supramolecular Diatomic Kagome Lattice
comment: 22 pages, 4 figures, published online in Nano Lett., https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.nanolett.6c03195
summary: Lattice geometry plays a fundamental role in the behavior of Bloch electrons in a crystal. The diatomic Kagome lattice, an extension of the honeycomb and Kagome lattices, is predicted to give rise to emergent and topological phenomena, but its experimental investigation has been limited thus far. Here, we fabricate a diatomic Kagome lattice through self-assembly of a triptycene derivative with phenazine moieties (Trip-Phz)---a $\mathrm{C_3}$-symmetric, non-planar $π$-conjugated molecule. Our scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) observations show that Trip-Phz forms a highly ordered diatomic Kagome lattice terminated by zigzag-type edges on the Pb(111) surface. Combined STM measurements and tight-binding calculations provide direct evidence for the existence of the edge states that correspond to those of graphene. These states are topological edge states dictated by the quantization of the Zak phase and the bulk-edge correspondence.This work reveals an ideal platform for exploring quantum materials with unique lattice geometries using supramolecular technology.

AI.method: Self-assembly of Trip-Phz (C3-symmetric non-planar pi-conjugated molecule) on Pb(111) surface to fabricate the diatomic Kagome lattice; characterization via scanning tunneling microscopy (STM); analysis combined with tight-binding calculations.
AI.result: STM reveals a highly ordered diatomic Kagome lattice terminated by zigzag-type edges on Pb(111). Combined STM and tight-binding calculations provide direct evidence of graphene-like edge states that are topological in nature, governed by Zak phase quantization and bulk-edge correspondence.

title: Decoding Oxygen K-edge Fingerprints of NCM-811 Degradation via Ab Initio Many-Body Theory and High-Throughput Screening of Crystal Proxies
summary: The degradation of LiNi$_{0.8}$Co$_{0.1}$Mn$_{0.1}$O$_2$ (NCM-811) in Li-ion batteries produces complex transition-metal oxides and binary phases that fundamentally limit cathode performance. While identifying these degradation products via X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) is essential for mitigating electrochemical performance loss, interpretation remains challenging due to the structural complexity of real-world samples. In this work, we present an integrated theoretical-experimental framework combining high-resolution oxygen K-edge XAS with \textit{ab initio} simulations based on many-body perturbation theory and high-throughput screening from density functional theory. We first evaluate the spectroscopic fingerprints of eight layered, spinel, and nominal rock-salt reference oxides, identifying discrepancies between the idealized single-crystal bulk phase and experimental spectra. Using high-throughput screening to analyze the oxygen $p$-projected density of states of 38 distinct polymorphs of NiO, CoO, and MnO, we propose that the spectral differences can emerge, among other factors, from a structural ensemble of local variations represented here by simplified structural proxies. Our work establishes a viable and rigorous computational pathway to interpret the complex landscape of degraded battery materials.

The authors evaluate spectroscopic fingerprints of eight reference oxides and use high-throughput analysis of 38 polymorphs of NiO, CoO, and MnO, proposing that spectral discrepancies arise from structural ensembles of local variations, establishing a rigorous computational pathway for interpreting degraded battery materials.
AI.motivation: The degradation of NCM-811 cathodes produces complex transition-metal oxides and binary phases that limit battery performance. While XAS is essential for identifying these degradation products, interpretation is challenging due to structural complexity of real-world samples, necessitating a reliable computational framework to connect experimental spectra to structural origins.

They evaluate spectroscopic fingerprints of eight layered, spinel, and rock-salt reference oxides, then analyze oxygen p-projected density of states of 38 polymorphs of NiO, CoO, and MnO using high-throughput screening, using simplified structural proxies to represent local structural variations.
