title: Nonreciprocal Magnon Hanle Effect in Antiferromagnetic $α$-Fe$_2$O$_3$
summary: The precession of the magnon pseudospin about the equilibrium pseudofield, the latter capturing the nature of magnonic eigenexcitations in an antiferromagnet, gives rise to the magnon Hanle effect. Its realization via electrically injected and detected spin transport in an antiferromagnetic insulator demonstrates its high potential for devices and as a convenient probe for magnon eigenmodes and the underlying spin interactions in the antiferromagnet. Here, we observe a non-reciprocity in the Hanle signal measured in alpha-Fe2O3 using two spatially separated Pt electrodes as spin injector and detector. Interchanging their roles alters the detected magnon spin signal. The recorded difference depends on the applied magnetic field and reverses sign when the signal passes its nominal maximum at the so-called compensation field. Our findings unlock the high potential of antiferromagnetic magnonics towards the realization of electronics-inspired phenomena.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the observation of non-reciprocity in the magnon Hanle effect signal in the antiferromagnetic insulator alpha-Fe2O3, using two separated Pt electrodes as spin injector and detector, where interchanging their roles alters the detected magnon spin signal.
AI.motivation: The magnon Hanle effect in antiferromagnets has high potential for devices and as a probe for magnon eigenmodes, but the authors aim to explore whether non-reciprocal behavior can be observed in this system and unlock electronics-inspired phenomena in antiferromagnetic magnonics.
AI.method: Electrical spin injection and detection using two spatially separated Pt electrodes on alpha-Fe2O3, measuring the Hanle signal and interchanging the roles of injector and detector to compare detected magnon spin signals under varying applied magnetic fields.
AI.result: A non-reciprocity in the Hanle signal is observed when interchanging injector and detector roles. The recorded difference depends on the applied magnetic field and reverses sign at the compensation field, where the signal passes its nominal maximum.
AI.conclusion: The findings demonstrate non-reciprocal magnon spin transport in antiferromagnets, unlocking the high potential of antiferromagnetic magnonics toward realizing electronics-inspired phenomena.

title: Linker Functionalization and pH Tuning Enhance Solar-Driven Catalytic CO$_2$ Reduction in MOF-5
summary: The wide band gap of metal-organic framework (MOF) 5 constrains its use in photocatalytic carbon dioxide (CO$_2$) reduction despite its high porosity and favorable mass-transport properties. Adopting a state-of-the-art first-principles approach, we systematically investigate the effects of volumetric strain, metal-node substitution, linker functionalization, and pH control as knobs to improve the CO$_2$ photocatalytic ability of MOF-5. Strain and metal-node substitution negligibly affect the gap, whereas linker functionalization narrows it into the visible range via in-gap states while preserving reduction-side alignment at pH = 0. The resulting reduction energetics are strongly sensitive to both linker functionalization and pH. Halogenated and hydroxylated frameworks provide access primarily to HCOOH, CO, and HCHO under alkaline conditions, principally with the Mg and Zn nodes, whereas COOH functionalization offers the broadest thermodynamic accessibility across the full CO$_2$ reduction sequence. NH$_2$ retains thermodynamic feasibility for all target reduction pathways but with larger overpotentials, while NO$_2$ generally yields unfavorable reduction energetics. Crucially, within the COOH series, the choice of the metal node tunes the fundamental gap by over 1 eV with only minor changes in the reduction overpotentials, placing Sr- and Ba-based architectures as the most favorable ones for broad product selectivity with visible-light excitation. Linker functionalization substantially reduces the spatial overlap of the frontier states, promoting photoinduced charge separation. Taken together, these results establish linker functionalization and solution pH as complementary design levers for independently tuning light absorption and CO$_2$-reduction energetics in MOF-5, establishing a rational and viable route for designing efficient MOF-based photocatalysts.

Linker functionalization narrows the band gap into the visible range and preserves favorable reduction alignment, while functional group and pH jointly control reduction energetics. COOH-functionalized frameworks with Sr/Ba nodes offer the broadest thermodynamic accessibility across the full CO2 reduction sequence with visible-light excitation.

AI.method: State-of-the-art first-principles DFT calculations systematically testing four knobs: volumetric strain, metal-node substitution, linker functionalization, and pH control, analyzing band gap, frontier-state overlap, and CO2 reduction thermodynamics.
AI.result: Strain and metal-node substitution barely affect the gap; linker functionalization narrows the gap into visible range via in-gap states while preserving reduction-side alignment at pH=0. Halogenated/hydroxylated frameworks access HCOOH/CO/HCHO under alkaline conditions mainly with Mg and Zn nodes; COOH functionalization gives broadest thermodynamic access to full reduction sequence; NH2 is feasible with larger overpotentials; NO2 is unfavorable. Within COOH series, metal-node choice tunes the gap by over 1 eV with minor overpotential changes, making Sr/Ba architectures most favorable. Linker functionalization reduces frontier-state spatial overlap, promoting charge separation.
AI.conclusion: Linker functionalization and solution pH are complementary independent design levers for tuning light absorption and CO2-reduction energetics in MOF-5, providing a rational route to efficient MOF-based photocatalysts.

title: Twist as a Mechanical Switch for Reconfigurable Stacking in h-BN
summary: Twistronics of layered materials has emerged as a highly active field due to its profound implications for quantum electronics and materials engineering. However, the controllable manipulation of interlayer stacking remains a significant experimental challenge. Here, the homogeneous contact between hexagonal boron nitride layers is shown to be reproducibly switched between two distinct stable stacking configurations via an externally applied torque. Combining experiments and computational modelling, we identify the stacking order of these stable states as the commensurate AA and AB modes. These two states are associated with different rotational torque maxima, exhibiting an asymmetry ratio of 0.7, and distinct dynamics as a function of the twist angle. Moreover, the peak torque values scale linearly with contact area, highlighting the dominant role of edge elasticity in the twisting process. Given that the AA and AB stacking modes correspond to different out-of-plane electric polarization states, our findings offer a pathway for reconfigurable nano- and micro-electromechanical devices.

The two states exhibit distinct rotational torque maxima (asymmetry ratio 0.7) and dynamics, with peak torque scaling linearly with contact area due to edge elasticity. This enables reconfigurable nano- and micro-electromechanical devices.
AI.motivation: While twistronics of layered materials holds great potential for quantum electronics and materials engineering, the controllable manipulation of interlayer stacking remains a significant experimental challenge that needs to be overcome.
AI.method: Combines experiments and computational modelling to apply externally applied torque to hexagonal boron nitride layers and analyze switching between stacking configurations. Structural identification uses commensurate AA and AB mode analysis, with torque measurement and scaling analysis against contact area.
AI.result: Homogeneous contact between hexagonal boron nitride layers can be reproducibly switched between AA and AB stable stacking configurations via external torque. The two states show different rotational torque maxima (asymmetry ratio ~0.7), distinct twist-angle-dependent dynamics, and peak torque scaling linearly with contact area, indicating dominant edge elasticity effects.
AI.conclusion: Since AA and AB stacking modes correspond to different out-of-plane electric polarization states, these findings offer a pathway for reconfigurable nano- and micro-electromechanical devices enabled by torque-controlled interlayer stacking manipulation.

title: Vitrification-Devitrification Enables Tunable Photonic and Gas Sorption Properties of Zeolitic Imidazolate Frameworks
summary: Zeolitic imidazolate framework (ZIF) glasses represent an emerging family of melt-quenched glasses, which exhibit immense potential for applications in gas separation, energy storage, and optics. However, their intrinsic porosity remains elusive due to the inherent challenges in resolving their disordered atomistic structures. Here, we systematically investigate the porosity of ZIF-4 and ZIF-62 crystals and their corresponding glasses. CO2 sorption at 195 K enables quantitative assessment of microporosity in both crystalline and glassy states, allowing the accessible micropore volume of the ZIF glasses to be determined. Moreover, establishing a direct relationship between photonic properties and structural porosity in Zn-based ZIF glasses remains challenging. Here we demonstrate striking broadband blue-light emission from ZIF-4 glass annealed under optimized conditions. A pronounced red shift is observed when increasing the annealing temperature above the glass transition temperature. By correlating the evolution of photoluminescence with structural porosity, we reveal the interplay between the photonic and gas sorption properties of ZIF glasses. These findings provide new insights into the structure-property relationships of ZIF glasses and offer a pathway toward the rational design of multifunctional MOF glasses.

AI.motivation: ZIF glasses are promising functional materials but their intrinsic porosity has remained unclear due to the difficulty of resolving disordered atomistic structures. Understanding porosity and linking it to photonic properties is essential for rational design of multifunctional MOF glasses.
AI.method: CO2 sorption measurements at 195 K were used to quantitatively assess microporosity in ZIF-4 and ZIF-62 crystals and their corresponding glasses, determining accessible micropore volumes. Photoluminescence spectroscopy was correlated with structural porosity evolution upon annealing ZIF-4 glass above its glass transition temperature.
AI.result: Quantitative micropore volumes were determined for both crystalline and glassy ZIF-4 and ZIF-62 states. Striking broadband blue-light emission was observed from ZIF-4 glass annealed under optimized conditions, with a pronounced red shift occurring as annealing temperature increased above the glass transition temperature. A direct correlation between photoluminescence evolution and structural porosity was established.
AI.conclusion: The findings reveal the interplay between photonic and gas sorption properties of ZIF glasses, providing new insights into structure-property relationships and offering a pathway toward rational design of multifunctional MOF glasses.

title: QArray+: A physics-informed GPU-accelerated simulator for quantum dot arrays
comment: P.V and B.v.S contributed equally to this work. 19 pages, 13 figures
summary: Semiconductor quantum-dot arrays are a compelling platform for scalable quantum technologies, yet their practical operation is hindered by the complexity of tuning large-scale devices. Existing automation tools rely on simplified physical models---such as constant-capacitance approximations and equilibrium Hubbard models---which assume instantaneous relaxation to a steady state. These frameworks fail in experimentally critical regimes where measurement rates exceed tunneling dynamics, necessitating more sophisticated non-equilibrium control strategies. To bridge this gap, we introduce QArray+, an extension of the QArray framework that incorporates gate-dependent tunnel coupling and a quantum open-system description of dissipative processes. This approach enables the unified simulation of coherent interdot charge-state hybridization and the non-equilibrium latching dynamics essential for training robust machine-learning models for automated device operation. Implemented in JAX with GPU acceleration, QArray+ scales across GPUs and multi-node systems. For example, a charge stability diagram for a 100X100 grid of gate voltages over 64 dots can be computed in $\sim0.17\,\mathrm{s}$ on multiple GPUs. Since interdot interactions are short-ranged and the corresponding tuning corrections are local, simulations at these scales capture the physics relevant to even larger devices. These capabilities support high-throughput dataset generation for automated device tuning.

AI.tldr: QArray+ extends the QArray framework for simulating semiconductor quantum-dot arrays by incorporating gate-dependent tunnel coupling and open-system (non-equilibrium) dissipative dynamics, enabling accurate simulation of coherent charge hybridization and latching behavior. It is implemented in JAX with GPU/multi-node scaling, computing a 100×100 charge stability diagram over 64 dots in ~0.17 s, supporting high-throughput dataset generation for automated device tuning.

These fail in experimentally relevant regimes where measurement rates exceed tunneling dynamics, requiring non-equilibrium control strategies that current simulators cannot capture.
AI.method: QArray+ augments the QArray framework with gate-dependent tunnel coupling and a quantum open-system description of dissipative processes, enabling unified simulation of coherent interdot charge-state hybridization and non-equilibrium latching dynamics. It is implemented in JAX and leverages GPU acceleration with scaling across GPUs and multi-node systems.

Because interdot interactions are short-ranged and tuning corrections local, simulations at this scale are representative of physics relevant to even larger devices.
AI.conclusion: QArray+ provides scalable, physically realistic simulation capabilities that support high-throughput dataset generation for training robust machine-learning models for automated quantum-device operation, addressing a critical gap in non-equilibrium tuning scenarios.

title: Ferroelastic domain switching by ultrafast photoinduced strain
summary: The crystal lattice underpins the fundamental properties of condensed matter, with ferroic order emerging sensitively from atomic coordination. Manipulating the lattic therefore promises a direct way to switch ferroics between their states. Infrared excitation provides an efficient pathway to drive lattice motion and generate transient crystal deformations and strains. Ferroelastics constitute a uniquely direct platform for such control, their order parameter being strain itself. However, whether ultrafast laser-induced lattice distortions can switch ferroelastic order remains unknown. Here we use ultrafast pump-probe microscopy to demonstrate that a single high-amplitude infrared pulse induces strain within the first nanosecond, followed by ferroelastic domain switching several nanoseconds later. The spatial distribution follows that expected from the photoinduced strain field, while their temporal evolution is closely coupled to the strain dynamics. Our observations identify transient strain as the driving field for ferroelastic switching and suggest a general lattice-mediated pathway for controlling ferroic order using infrared light.

AI.tldr: Using ultrafast pump-probe microscopy, the authors demonstrate that a single high-amplitude infrared pulse induces strain within the first nanosecond, followed by ferroelastic domain switching several nanoseconds later, identifying transient strain as the driving field for ferroelastic switching.
AI.motivation: Manipulating the crystal lattice promises a direct way to switch ferroic states between their phases, and infrared excitation offers an efficient pathway to drive lattice motion. Ferroelastics, whose order parameter is strain itself, constitute a uniquely direct platform for such control; however, whether ultrafast laser-induced lattice distortions can actually switch ferroelastic order was previously unknown.
AI.method: The authors used ultrafast pump-probe microscopy to excite the material with a single high-amplitude infrared pulse and temporally resolved the induced strain and subsequent ferroelastic domain switching dynamics.
AI.result: A single high-amplitude infrared pulse induces strain within the first nanosecond, followed by ferroelastic domain switching several nanoseconds later. The spatial distribution of switching matches the expected photoinduced strain field, and the temporal evolution is closely coupled to strain dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Transient strain is identified as the driving field for ferroelastic switching, suggesting a general lattice-mediated pathway for controlling ferroic order using infrared light.

title: Emergence of the magnetic octupole Rashba-Edelstein effect from spin-orbit entanglement
summary: Magnetic multipoles have attracted growing interest as order parameters and dynamical degrees of freedom in unconventional magnets, yet it remains unclear how broadly they can emerge as active electronic degrees of freedom. Here, we show that spin-orbit-entangled multiorbital states can host magnetic octupole (MO) degrees of freedom. In Rashba systems, this gives rise to an MO Rashba texture accompanying the J-Rashba texture. Remarkably, spin-orbital entanglement can realize a pure-MO limit in which the spin and orbital-angular-momentum textures vanish while the MO texture remains finite. An applied electric field converts this texture into a nonequilibrium MO polarization through an MO Rashba-Edelstein effect. Around the pure-MO regime, the MO Edelstein response dominates over the conventional spin response, showing that multipolar responses need not be small corrections to dipolar spin physics. Our results establish an interface-based route for electrically generating nonequilibrium multipolar magnetic polarization in spin-orbit-coupled systems.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that spin-orbit-entangled multiorbital states can host magnetic octupole (MO) degrees of freedom, leading to an MO Rashba texture in Rashba systems. Through spin-orbital entanglement, a pure-MO limit is achievable where spin and orbital angular momentum textures vanish while MO texture remains. An applied electric field generates nonequilibrium MO polarization via an MO Rashba-Edelstein effect, which can dominate over conventional spin response near the pure-MO regime. This establishes an interface-based route for electrically generating nonequilibrium multipolar magnetic polarization.
AI.motivation: To determine how broadly magnetic multipoles can emerge as active electronic degrees of freedom in unconventional magnets, beyond their known roles as order parameters and dynamical degrees of freedom.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis demonstrating that spin-orbit-entangled multiorbital states can host magnetic octupole degrees of freedom, examining Rashba systems for MO Rashba textures and analyzing the electric-field-induced MO Rashba-Edelstein effect toward a pure-MO limit.
AI.result: A pure-MO limit is realized through spin-orbital entanglement where spin and orbital angular momentum textures vanish but MO texture survives. An MO Rashba-Edelstein effect converts electric fields into nonequilibrium MO polarization, and the MO Edelstein response dominates over the conventional spin response near the pure-MO regime.
AI.conclusion: Multipolar responses need not be small corrections to dipolar spin physics, and the findings establish an interface-based route for electrically generating nonequilibrium multipolar magnetic polarization in spin-orbit-coupled systems.

title: Magneto-Structural Coupling Enables Cryogenic Cation Redistribution in a Spinel Oxide
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures. Submitted to National Science Review
summary: Ionic transport in oxides is generally frozen at cryogenic temperatures, where thermal energy lies far below typical cation-migration barriers. Neutron powder diffraction reveals progressive Fe/Mg redistribution between tetrahedral (A) and octahedral (B) sites in the spinel Mg0.5Fe0.5TiFeO4 upon cooling from 200 K to 5 K. A-site Fe occupancy increases toward near completion at 5 K within Rietveld resolution, while Ti remains on the B site. This exchange coincides with complex magnetic correlations rather than a classical thermally activated window. Low-temperature magnetostrictive volume changes indicate strong spin-lattice coupling, but do not identify magnetostriction as the sole thermodynamic driver. Room-temperature high-pressure X-ray diffraction produces the opposite occupancy trend, showing that volume contraction alone cannot explain the cryogenic site exchange. These results point to magneto-structural free-energy minimization as a plausible mechanism for unlocking cryogenic cation mobility in a correlated spinel oxide.

AI.tldr: Neutron and X-ray diffraction studies reveal progressive Fe/Mg cation redistribution between tetrahedral and octahedral sites in the spinel Mg0.5Fe0.5TiFeO4 upon cooling to 5 K, despite cryogenic temperatures where cation migration is normally frozen. This anomalous low-temperature ionic exchange correlates with magnetic ordering and magnetostriction rather than thermal activation, suggesting magneto-structural free-energy minimization drives the cryogenic cation mobility.
AI.motivation: Ionic transport in oxides is conventionally expected to be frozen at cryogenic temperatures because thermal energy lies far below typical cation-migration barriers. This study investigates the surprising observation of progressive Fe/Mg redistribution between crystallographic sites down to 5 K, aiming to understand the physical mechanism enabling such low-temperature cation mobility.
AI.method: The authors use neutron powder diffraction to track Fe/Mg site occupancy as a function of temperature from 200 K to 5 K, complemented by room-temperature high-pressure X-ray diffraction to probe the effect of volume contraction on site occupancy, along with analysis of magnetic correlations and magnetostrictive volume changes to assess spin-lattice coupling.

The exchange coincides with complex magnetic correlations rather than a thermally activated process. Low-temperature magnetostrictive volume changes show strong spin-lattice coupling but are not the sole thermodynamic driver, as high-pressure X-ray diffraction at room temperature produces the opposite occupancy trend.

The results indicate that magneto-structural free-energy minimization is a plausible mechanism for enabling cryogenic cation mobility in this correlated spinel oxide, offering a new paradigm beyond conventional thermally activated ionic transport.

title: Relaxation effects on Hartree-Fock ground states in twisted bilayer graphene at even integer fillings
summary: A standard approach for studying magic angle twisted bilayer graphene (MATBG)'s correlated electronic phase diagram is to project the Coulomb interaction down to effective models only involving electrons in single-particle flat bands and some nearby remote bands. We provide a novel systematic derivation of a single-particle continuum model of MATBG's single-particle properties which incorporates structural relaxation while remaining in the Lagrangian frame. We project the Coulomb interactions down to electrons occupying the flat bands of this model and compute the Hartree-Fock many-body ground states at fillings $ν= \pm 2$. We find that incorporating relaxation effects drives the model into a semi-metallic phase at $- 2$ because of particle-hole asymmetry in the relaxed model's single-particle dispersion and because the flat band wavefunctions become more concentrated leading to an enhanced Hartree potential. Our results corroborate recent ab initio density functional theory studies which also found semi-metallic phases at $-2$. We discuss potential explanations for why such phases have not been seen in experiments.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a systematic derivation of a single-particle continuum model for MATBG that incorporates structural relaxation in the Lagrangian frame. By projecting Coulomb interactions onto the flat-band electrons and computing Hartree-Fock ground states at fillings ν=±2, the authors find that relaxation effects drive the model into a semi-metallic phase at ν=-2, due to particle-hole asymmetry and enhanced Hartree potential from more concentrated flat-band wavefunctions. This corroborates recent DFT studies and the authors discuss why such semi-metallic phases have not been experimentally observed.
AI.motivation: The standard approach to studying MATBG's correlated phases involves projecting Coulomb interactions onto flat-band effective models. The authors aim to provide a more accurate continuum model that systematically incorporates structural relaxation, as relaxation effects may significantly alter single-particle dispersion and many-body physics but are often neglected or treated improperly in effective models.
AI.method: The authors derive a single-particle continuum model of MATBG that includes structural relaxation while remaining in the Lagrangian frame. They project Coulomb interactions onto the flat bands of this relaxed model and compute Hartree-Fock many-body ground states at fillings ν=±2, examining the effects of relaxation on single-particle dispersion, wavefunction localization, and the Hartree potential.
AI.result: Incorporating relaxation drives the model into a semi-metallic phase at filling ν=-2, due to particle-hole asymmetry in the relaxed single-particle dispersion and enhanced Hartree potential caused by more concentrated flat-band wavefunctions. These results corroborate recent ab initio DFT studies that also found semi-metallic phases at ν=-2.
AI.conclusion: The findings suggest that structural relaxation is crucial for accurately modeling MATBG's correlated phases at negative fillings, aligning with DFT predictions of semi-metallic behavior. The authors discuss potential explanations (e.g., experimental factors or model limitations) for why such semi-metallic phases have not been observed in experiments.

title: Molecular-dynamics-based modal analysis of heat transport in quasi-one-dimensional systems from a symmetry-adapted perspective
summary: Detailed analysis of thermal conductivity results obtained from molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories conventionally relies on knowledge of the harmonic vibrational modes of the system. Such is the case in methods like Green--Kubo modal analysis (GKMA) and homogeneous nonequilibrium modal analysis (HNEMA). This approach faces several shortcomings that become especially important when dealing with nanostructures. Chief among them is scalability, followed by the ambiguity associated to the degeneracy of the large vibrational subspaces defined by a common translational wave number k. We propose an alternative for quasi-one-dimensional (quasi-1D) systems: we construct the modal basis for the decomposition of the thermal conductivity from line-group projection operators, so that every projected component carries well-defined symmetry labels (including rotational information and parities) and the decomposition is unique at the level of irreducible representations (irreps). Applying the idea to a (10,0)-(20,0) WS2-MoS2 double-walled nanotube (DWNT) described by a neuroevolution potential (NEP), we find that at 300 K both HNEMA and GKMA yield statistically consistent total conductivities and allow the identification of several prominent symmetry-adapted conduction channels. The GKMA pair matrix shows that within-block and same-channel cross-k terms account for 75.6% of the total conductivity, while cross-channel correlations contribute 24.4%.

AI.tldr: The authors propose a line-group symmetry-based modal decomposition method for analyzing thermal conductivity in quasi-1D systems, replacing conventional harmonic mode analysis that suffers from scalability and degeneracy issues. Applied to a (10,0)-(20,0) WS2-MoS2 double-walled nanotube using a neuroevolution potential, both HNEMA and GKMA yield consistent total conductivities at 300 K, with intra-channel and same-channel cross-k terms contributing 75.6% of total conductivity.
AI.motivation: Conventional MD-based thermal conductivity analysis relies on harmonic vibrational modes (used in GKMA and HNEMA), which faces scalability challenges and degeneracy ambiguity in vibrational subspaces associated with translational wave numbers, especially problematic for nanostructures.
AI.method: The authors construct the modal basis for thermal conductivity decomposition using line-group projection operators for quasi-1D systems. Every projected component carries well-defined symmetry labels (including rotational information and parities), and the decomposition is unique at the level of irreducible representations.
AI.result: At 300 K, both HNEMA and GKMA produce statistically consistent total thermal conductivities for a (10,0)-(20,0) WS2-MoS2 DWNT described by a neuroevolution potential. GKMA pair matrix analysis shows within-block and same-channel cross-k terms account for 75.6% of total conductivity, while cross-channel correlations contribute 24.4%. Several prominent symmetry-adapted conduction channels were identified.
AI.conclusion: Line-group symmetry projection provides a scalable, unambiguous alternative to harmonic-mode-based modal analysis for quasi-1D thermal conductivity decomposition, enabling unique symmetry-labeled channel identification and a clearer interpretation of phonon conduction mechanisms in nanostructures.

title: Chemical pressure and vacancies in crystals under nonhydrostatic stress
summary: Inhomogeneous stress is a driving force for diffusion of vacancies in crystals. The other way around a non-uniform distribution of vacancies induces stress. The accepted theory of composition-stress coupling in crystals is Larché-Cahn (LC) theory. Composition is defined in terms of the population of lattice sites with a limit of one-particle per site. Coupling is modelled by adding a compositional strain term to the elastic strain in the constitutive relation for stress. An alternative mechanism, proposed here, is letting the site binding energy vary with spatial (deformed) density. This generates a chemical pressure adding to the elastic stress. The governing equations for this model are derived using non-equilibrium continuum thermodynamic methods. The gradient of the chemical pressure has a dual function acting both as the drift force for migration and as an effective internal one body force in the Cauchy equation for the elastic stress. The practical evaluation presented in the paper is restricted to equilibrium properties. We examine the effect of externally applied non-hydrostatic stress, either in the form of surface tractions or a one-body force density (gravitation). The model system is a one component crystal with a fixed number of lattice sites. The number of particles can be variable but is always smaller than the number of lattice sites. The linear elastic response is modelled by the standard Lamé stress tensor. The results for systems deformed by surface tractions are in qualitative agreement with LC theory allowing for differences in the expression for the elastic moduli. Deviations are more serious for the crystal deformed by gravitation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an alternative mechanism to the Larché-Cahn theory for composition-stress coupling in crystals, where site binding energy varies with deformed spatial density rather than adding compositional strain to elastic strain, generating a "chemical pressure." The model is derived via non-equilibrium continuum thermodynamics, with the chemical pressure gradient acting as both drift force for vacancy migration and an effective body force in the elastic Cauchy equation. Equilibrium results under non-hydrostatic stress show qualitative agreement with LC theory for surface tractions but larger deviations for gravitational deformation.
AI.motivation: Inhomogeneous stress drives vacancy diffusion in crystals, and non-uniform vacancy distributions induce stress. The accepted Larché-Cahn (LC) theory models this coupling by adding compositional strain to elastic strain, but this mechanism has limitations. The authors propose an alternative coupling mechanism where site binding energy varies with deformed spatial density, generating a chemical pressure that adds to elastic stress.
AI.method: Governing equations are derived using non-equilibrium continuum thermodynamic methods. The model considers a one-component crystal with fixed lattice sites and variable particle number (always fewer than sites). The chemical pressure gradient serves dual roles: as drift force for migration and as an effective internal body force in the Cauchy equation. Linear elastic response is modeled with the standard Lamé stress tensor. Equilibrium properties are evaluated under externally applied non-hydrostatic stress from surface tractions or a one-body force density (gravitation).
AI.result: For systems deformed by surface tractions, results are in qualitative agreement with LC theory, with differences appearing only in the expressions for elastic moduli. More serious deviations from LC theory occur for the crystal deformed by gravitation, indicating the alternative mechanism yields distinct predictions in bulk-force scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The proposed binding-energy-density coupling mechanism provides an alternative framework for composition-stress coupling in crystals. It reproduces LC theory qualitatively under surface traction loading but diverges more substantially under body-force (gravitational) loading, suggesting the two mechanisms are not fully equivalent and have experimentally distinguishable consequences.

title: Spin wave freezing in Re/Co/Pt multilayers
comment: Accepted for publication in Physical Review B
summary: The phenomenon of spin wave (SW) freezing occurs in the Damon-Eshbach mode in thin film magnetic systems, when SW phase and group velocities both go to zero, and the wave ceases to oscillate and move, preserving its shape as a domain structure pattern. This effect is related to the spin reorientation transition, where the magnetization configuration changes between the homogeneous in-plane state and domain structure with the out-of-plane magnetization component state. Here, we study the SW freezing effect in [Re/Co/Pt]$_{20}$ magnetic multilayers, induced by varying the in-plane external magnetic field. The studies were performed on nanostructures with the quality factor $Q$ (ratio of uniaxial anisotropy to demagnetization energies) greater and smaller than one. Domain structures with an out-of-plane magnetization component were observed in these multilayers. The critical field, visible as the saturation field $H_s^{||}$ in the parallel static magnetization curve measured by superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID), is also manifested in the field-dependent vector-network-analyzer ferromagnetic resonance (VNA-FMR) experiment, which measures the homogeneous magnetization oscillations. Brillouin Light Scattering (BLS) spectra, recorded for several values of wave vectors and several field values, probed the field-evolution of the dispersion relation. Micromagnetic simulations allow one to obtain a full dispersion, in good agreement with VNA-FMR and BLS results. Around $H_s^{||}$ the simulated dispersion relations approach the conditions for SW freezing. Below $H_s^{||}$ low and high frequency VNA-FMR modes are related to magnetization oscillations inside domain walls and within domains, respectively. The experimental results of static and dynamic behavior, together with micromagnetic simulations, create an overall consistent picture of the investigated multilayers.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates spin wave (SW) freezing in the Damon-Eshbach mode within [Re/Co/Pt]20 magnetic multilayers by varying an in-plane external magnetic field. Combining SQUID magnetometry, VNA-FMR, Brillouin Light Scattering, and micromagnetic simulations, the authors show that near the saturation field Hs||, the dispersion relations approach conditions for SW freezing, and domain structures with out-of-plane magnetization components play a key role in this phenomenon.
AI.motivation: To understand and characterize the spin wave freezing effect in magnetic multilayers, where SW phase and group velocities vanish near the spin reorientation transition—a phenomenon related to the change in magnetization configuration between a homogeneous in-plane state and a domain structure with out-of-plane components.
AI.method: Experiments were performed on [Re/Co/Pt]20 multilayers with quality factor Q greater and smaller than one. Static magnetization was measured via SQUID, dynamic magnetic properties via vector-network-analyzer ferromagnetic resonance (VNA-FMR), dispersion relations were probed using Brillouin Light Scattering (BLS) at several wave vectors and fields, and micromagnetic simulations provided full dispersion relations.
AI.result: Domain structures with out-of-plane magnetization components were observed. The critical saturation field Hs|| from SQUID measurements is also manifested in VNA-FMR experiments. Simulated dispersion relations approach SW freezing conditions around Hs||. Below Hs||, low and high frequency VNA-FMR modes correspond to magnetization oscillations inside domain walls and within domains, respectively. Simulations agree well with VNA-FMR and BLS data.
AI.conclusion: The static and dynamic experimental results, combined with micromagnetic simulations, form a consistent picture of SW freezing in these multilayers, demonstrating that SW freezing conditions are approached near the saturation field via tuning of the in-plane magnetic field.

title: 'pySNOW': a Python Suite for the NanO-World
summary: In computational materials science, numerical simulations are indispensable tools for revealing atomic-scale processes. For building blocks of the nanoworld, such as nanoparticles and nanoalloys, atomistic simulations provide detailed insight into their behaviour under diverse conditions. These simulations enable the study of formation and growth mechanisms, transport phenomena, chemophysical stability, and chemical reactions, including catalytic processes. To unravel the complex structure--property relationships that characterise nanoobjects, it is crucial to develop robust and insightful representations of their atomistic structure at global and local scales. Such descriptions enhance our understanding of nanoparticle behaviour and play a key role in guiding their rational design in silico for targeted applications.

AI.tldr: This paper discusses the role of atomistic simulations in computational materials science for studying nanoparticles and nanoalloys, emphasizing the need for robust structural representations to link structure with properties for rational nanomaterial design.
AI.motivation: Numerical simulations are essential for revealing atomic-scale processes in nanoparticles and nanoalloys, but complex structure-property relationships require robust and insightful representations of atomistic structure at global and local scales to enable rational in silico design.
AI.method: The paper emphasizes the use of atomistic simulations to study formation/growth mechanisms, transport phenomena, chemophysical stability, and chemical reactions (including catalysis), combined with structural descriptors that capture both global and local features of nanoobjects.
AI.result: No explicit quantitative results are presented in the abstract; instead, it argues that improved representations of atomistic structure enhance understanding and guide rational design of nanoparticles.
AI.conclusion: Developing robust and insightful representations of atomistic structure is crucial for unraveling structure-property relationships in nanoobjects and enabling their rational design in silico for targeted applications.

title: Spin Hall Magnetoresistance in Antiferromagnetic Insulators
summary: Antiferromagnetic materials promise improved performance for spintronic applications, as they are robust against external magnetic field perturbations and allow for faster magnetization dynamics compared to ferromagnets. The direct observation of the antiferromagnetic state, however, is challenging due to the absence of a macroscopic magnetization. We show that the spin Hall magnetoresistance (SMR) is a versatile tool to probe the antiferromagnetic spin structure via simple electrical transport experiments by investigating the easy-plane antiferromagnetic insulators alpha-Fe2O3 (hematite) and NiO in bilayer heterostructures with a Pt heavy-metal top electrode. While rotating an external magnetic field in three orthogonal planes, we record the longitudinal and the transverse resistivities of Pt and observe characteristic resistivity modulations consistent with the SMR effect. We analyze both their amplitude and phase and compare the data to the results from a prototypical collinear ferrimagnetic Y3Fe5O12/Pt bilayer. The observed magnetic field dependence is explained in a comprehensive model, based on two magnetic sublattices and taking into account magnetic field-induced modifications of the domain structure. Our results show that the SMR effect allows to readout the spin configuration and to investigate magnetoelastic effects in antiferromagnetic multi-domain materials. We demonstrate that the SMR amplitude scales with the sum of the absolute sublattice magnetizations in ferrimagnetic and antiferromagnetic materials. In alpha-Fe2O3/Pt bilayers, we find an unexpectedly large SMR amplitude of 2.5E-3, twice as high as for prototype Y3Fe5O12/Pt bilayers, making the system particularly interesting for room-temperature antiferromagnetic spintronic applications.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that spin Hall magnetoresistance (SMR) can be used as a versatile electrical transport technique to probe the antiferromagnetic spin structure in easy-plane antiferromagnetic insulators (alpha-Fe2O3 and NiO) via Pt bilayer heterostructures. The authors observe characteristic resistivity modulations consistent with the SMR effect, explain the magnetic field dependence using a two-sublattice model incorporating field-induced domain modifications, and find that alpha-Fe2O3/Pt exhibits an unexpectedly large SMR amplitude of 2.5E-3—twice that of the prototypical Y3Fe5O12/Pt—making it promising for room-temperature antiferromagnetic spintronics.
AI.motivation: Directly observing the antiferromagnetic state is challenging due to the absence of macroscopic magnetization, yet antiferromagnets promise improved spintronic performance—robustness against magnetic field perturbations and faster magnetization dynamics. A simple, versatile electrical probe of antiferromagnetic spin structure is needed.
AI.method: The authors measure longitudinal and transverse resistivities of Pt in bilayers of easy-plane antiferromagnetic insulators (alpha-Fe2O3 and NiO) with a Pt heavy-metal top electrode while rotating an external magnetic field in three orthogonal planes. They analyze amplitude and phase of the SMR-induced resistivity modulations, compare to a Y3Fe5O12/Pt ferrimagnetic reference, and develop a comprehensive two-sublattice model accounting for field-induced domain structure modifications.
AI.result: Characteristic SMR resistivity modulations are observed in both antiferromagnets, consistent with predictions. The model explains the magnetic field dependence, showing SMR amplitude scales with the sum of the absolute sublattice magnetizations. In alpha-Fe2O3/Pt, an unexpectedly large SMR amplitude of 2.5E-3 is found—twice that of Y3Fe5O12/Pt—which enables readout of spin configuration and investigation of magnetoelastic effects in antiferromagnetic multi-domain materials.
AI.conclusion: The SMR effect is a versatile electrical transport tool for probing antiferromagnetic spin structures and magnetoelastic effects. The large SMR amplitude in alpha-Fe2O3/Pt makes this system particularly interesting for room-temperature antiferromagnetic spintronic applications.

title: From Goldene to Noblene: exhaustive enumeration of the ordered Au-Ag-Cu monolayer alloys
summary: Two-dimensional metals became a laboratory reality with the isolation of Goldene, a gold sheet one atom thick released by chemical exfoliation, which raises the question of what alloying can achieve on the same close-packed lattice. Here we combine an exhaustive enumeration of derivative superstructures with density functional theory to map the ordered Au-Ag-Cu monolayer alloys, relaxing every symmetry-inequivalent arrangement up to four atoms per cell and extending the set with larger cells selected by a fitted model. We find that the arrangement of the atoms, and not their proportion, controls the mixing energy, since the spread among the orderings of a single composition is several times the step between neighboring compositions, one composition spans more than 50~meV/atom between two arrangements of the same three atoms, and at two compositions the arrangement decides the sign. The energetics is carried by a competition between Au-Cu contacts, which bind, and Ag-Cu contacts, which do not, and bulk enthalpies computed under the same protocol show that this chemistry is not uniformly rescaled in two dimensions, since Au-Cu orders more strongly in the monolayer than in the crystal while the other two weaken. A pair model completed by an elastic size-mismatch term reproduces the computed energies to a few meV/atom and returns a composition landscape whose convex hull no balanced ternary composition reaches. One equimolar ordering, which we name Noblene, is the only structure in which every atom is surrounded exclusively by unlike species, and it is dynamically stable and metallic, and carries a Poisson's ratio above one half, higher than that of any of the three pure monolayers. Since Noblene sits on the lattice that Goldene already realizes, the route that produced Goldene is a plausible starting point for its synthesis.

AI.tldr: The paper comprehensively maps ordered Au-Ag-Cu monolayer alloys via enumeration and DFT, finding that atomic arrangement (not composition) controls mixing energy, identifying a size-mismatch pair model that reproduces energetics, and discovering "Noblene"—an equimolar ordering where every atom has only unlike neighbors—which is dynamically stable, metallic, and exhibits a Poisson's ratio above 1/2, with a plausible synthesis route via the Goldene exfoliation method.
AI.motivation: With the isolation of Goldene (an atomically thin gold sheet by chemical exfoliation), the authors are motivated to explore what alloying can achieve on the same close-packed two-dimensional lattice, investigating whether mixed Au-Ag-Cu monolayers can yield structures with novel or enhanced properties.
AI.method: The authors combine exhaustive enumeration of derivative superstructures (relaxing all symmetry-inequivalent arrangements up to four atoms per cell, extending to larger cells via a fitted model) with density functional theory, and they benchmark monolayer energetics against bulk enthalpies under the same computational protocol. A pair interaction model augmented by an elastic size-mismatch term is fitted to reproduce the DFT energies.
AI.result: The mixing energy is governed by atomic arrangement rather than composition; spreads among orderings of a single composition exceed inter-composition steps, with one composition spanning >50 meV/atom and two compositions where arrangement determines the sign of mixing energy. The energetics stem from binding Au-Cu contacts versus non-binding Ag-Cu contacts, and this chemistry is not uniformly rescaled in 2D relative to bulk (Au-Cu orders more strongly in monolayers; the other pairs weaken). The pair + size-mismatch model fits to a few meV/atom, and no balanced ternary composition lies on the convex hull. The equimolar ordering "Noblene" has every atom surrounded exclusively by unlike species and is dynamically stable, metallic, with a Poisson's ratio above 1/2 exceeding all three pure monolayers.
AI.conclusion: Arrangement, not composition, dominates the energetics of Au-Ag-Cu monolayer alloys. Noblene is a uniquely ordered structure with every atom surrounded by unlike species, is stable and metallic, and possesses an unusually high Poisson's ratio; since it shares the lattice with Goldene, the same exfoliation route is a plausible synthetic pathway.

title: Colossal reversible conductivity switching by room-temperature oxygen-vacancy ordering in Aurivillius oxide films
summary: Oxygen vacancies are central to the functionality of oxides, yet they typically exist as randomly distributed point defects, limiting the ability to precisely manipulate their collective behavior. Here, we report the room-temperature formation of a long-range-ordered oxygen-vacancy superstructure in single-crystalline Aurivillius-phase Bi2WO6 thin films via a mild nitrogen-plasma treatment. This structural transformation unlocks a colossal, reversible modulation of electrical conductivity by more than nine orders of magnitude, accompanied by a striking optical transition from transparent to black. Atomic-resolution imaging and spectroscopy reveal that the vacancies selectively order within the perovskite-like tungsten oxide layers, forming a coherent defect lattice that is absent in the pristine film. Oxygen-plasma treatment removes the vacancy superstructure and restores the initial state, whereas subsequent nitrogen-plasma treatment reconstructs it, enabling repeatable room-temperature switching between distinct structural, electronic and optical states. The phenomenon is also observed in another Aurivillius member, Bi2MoO6, suggesting its generality across the Aurivillius family. These findings establish a new paradigm for atomic-scale defect engineering - using gentle plasma chemistry to construct ordered defect lattices, opening avenues for reversible property modulation in complex oxides.

AI.tldr: A mild nitrogen-plasma treatment induces room-temperature formation of a long-range-ordered oxygen-vacancy superstructure in Aurivillius-phase Bi2WO6 thin films, enabling colossal reversible electrical conductivity modulation (>9 orders of magnitude) and transparent-to-black optical switching. The phenomenon extends to Bi2MoO6, suggesting generality across the Aurivillius family.
AI.motivation: Oxygen vacancies are critical to oxide functionality but typically exist as randomly distributed point defects, which prevents precise control over their collective behavior. The authors seek to overcome this limitation by constructing ordered oxygen-vacancy lattices rather than relying on statistical defect distributions.
AI.method: Single-crystalline Aurivillius-phase Bi2WO6 thin films are treated with a mild nitrogen plasma at room temperature to induce vacancy ordering. Characterization employs atomic-resolution imaging and spectroscopy to visualize the vacancy superstructure within perovskite-like WO layers. Reversibility is achieved by alternating oxygen-plasma (removal) and nitrogen-plasma (reconstruction) treatments.
AI.result: The structural transformation triggers a colossal, reversible electrical conductivity change exceeding nine orders of magnitude and a transparent-to-black optical transition. Vacancies selectively order within the perovskite-like tungsten oxide layers, forming a coherent defect lattice. Switching between structural, electronic, and optical states is repeatable at room temperature. The same phenomenon is observed in Bi2MoO6, another Aurivillius member.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes a new paradigm for atomic-scale defect engineering using gentle plasma chemistry to construct ordered defect lattices in complex oxides, opening avenues for reversible property modulation and suggesting broad applicability across the Aurivillius family and potentially other oxide systems.

title: Understanding Graphene-Perovskite Interactions: From Flake Chemistry to Crystallisation and Solar Cell Performance
comment: 4 figures in main; 21 figures and 3 tables in the SI
summary: Graphene-derivatives are widely employed materials to improve bulk and interface properties of metal-halide perovskite devices. Yet the implications of their flake chemistry and interactions with the perovskite precursors remain unclear. Here, we show that pristine graphene flakes (GF) and more conventional graphene oxide flakes (GOF) are not interchangeable. Density functional theory calculations reveal that GOF interacts more strongly with the perovskite lattice but induces larger structural distortions, stronger interfacial polarisation, and localised gap states. In contrast, GF forms comparatively non-disruptive contacts, a response retained across a wide compositional range. Machine-learning atomistic simulations further show that GF contacts both Pb- and I-containing regions of solvated perovskite nanocrystals, with a strong solvent dependency. Solution spectroscopic characterization indicates that GF additives serve as scaffold for preorganised Pb/I-containing precursors, favouring film crystallisation. In this sense, GF enhances solar cell performance across perovskite compositions, but particularly those facing a more challenging crystallisation. In mixed Sn-Pb perovskite solar cells, GF raises the champion power-conversion efficiency from 21.5\% to 23.7\% with improved storage stability. These results establish pristine GF as a chemically defined additive and connect its atomic-scale interactions with precursor organisation, crystallisation, device performance, and stability.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that pristine graphene flakes (GF) and graphene oxide flakes (GOF) are not interchangeable additives in metal-halide perovskite solar cells. DFT calculations show GOF disrupts the perovskite lattice more severely, while GF forms non-disruptive contacts. GF scaffolds preorganized Pb/I precursors, improving crystallization and boosting mixed Sn-Pb perovskite solar cell efficiency from 21.5% to 23.7% with enhanced stability.
AI.motivation: Graphene derivatives are widely used to improve metal-halide perovskite device properties, but the influence of their flake chemistry and interactions with perovskite precursors remains unclear. The authors aim to clarify whether different graphene-based additives (pristine flakes vs. oxide flakes) behave distinctly and how their atomic-scale interactions affect crystallization, performance, and stability.
AI.method: The study combines density functional theory (DFT) calculations to compare GOF and GF interactions with the perovskite lattice, machine-learning atomistic simulations to probe GF contacts with solvated perovskite nanocrystals, and solution spectroscopic characterization alongside device fabrication to assess crystallization and solar cell performance across various perovskite compositions, including mixed Sn-Pb systems.
AI.result: GOF interacts more strongly with perovskite but induces larger structural distortions, stronger interfacial polarization, and localized gap states. GF forms comparatively non-disruptive contacts across a wide compositional range and scaffolds preorganized Pb/I-containing precursors, favoring film crystallization. In mixed Sn-Pb solar cells, GF increased champion power-conversion efficiency from 21.5% to 23.7% and improved storage stability.
AI.conclusion: Pristine GF is established as a chemically well-defined additive whose atomic-scale interactions are connected to precursor organization, crystallization, device performance, and stability, demonstrating that it outperforms GOF, particularly in challenging perovskite compositions.

title: Systematic display of the spin splitting in band structures of representative altermagnetic crystals
summary: In this work we demonstrate a novel approach to exhibit the unique spin splitting that is typical of collinear altermagnets. This approach is to plot band structures on Brillouin zone paths that sample general k-points to show a representative picture that corresponds to Brillouin zone averages. This is in contrast to conventional band structure plotting which plots band structures on the highest-symmetry points and lines, and thus in many cases can fail to show any altermagnetic spin splitting at all. Our investigation compares the new approach with the band structures of collinear altermagnets using conventional band structure plotting. We report the band structure and symmetry analysis for MnTe, CrSb, SmFeO3, ScCrO3, LaMnO3, TlCrO3, HoFeO3, InCrO3 and DyFeO3. This result clearly demonstrates the advantage of this novel method for displaying the spin splitting of collinear altermagnets.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a novel band structure plotting approach for collinear altermagnets that samples general k-points along Brillouin zone paths (representative of BZ averages) rather than conventional high-symmetry paths, which often fail to show altermagnetic spin splitting. The method is demonstrated on nine materials (MnTe, CrSb, SmFeO3, ScCrO3, LaMnO3, TlCrO3, HoFeO3, InCrO3, DyFeO3), showing clear advantage over conventional plotting.
AI.motivation: Conventional band structure plotting along high-symmetry points/lines frequently fails to reveal the unique spin splitting characteristic of collinear altermagnets, since this splitting often occurs away from high-symmetry directions. A method that samples general k-points is needed to display the altermagnetic spin-splitting signature.
AI.method: The authors propose plotting band structures on Brillouin zone paths that sample general (non-high-symmetry) k-points, providing a representative picture corresponding to Brillouin zone averages. This is compared against conventional band structure plotting along high-symmetry paths, combined with band structure and symmetry analysis for nine collinear altermagnetic materials.
AI.result: For all nine studied materials (MnTe, CrSb, and several rare-earth/transition-metal perovskites), the novel general-k-path approach clearly reveals altermagnetic spin splitting, whereas conventional high-symmetry band structure plots in many cases fail to show any splitting.
AI.conclusion: The general-k-point Brillouin zone sampling method is a superior approach for visually representing the spin splitting of collinear altermagnets, and it provides a more reliable representative picture of the BZ-averaged electronic structure than conventional high-symmetry band plotting.

title: AlterSeeK-Path: Systematic construction of generalized band-structure paths for displaying altermagnetic spin splitting
summary: Altermagnetic materials exhibit spin splitting in their electronic band structures while maintaining zero net magnetization. However, conventional high-symmetry k-paths generally hide this splitting because they follow symmetry lines that in most cases enforce spin degeneracy. We present AlterSeeK-Path, an open-source Python tool that systematically constructs generalized band-structure paths for collinear altermagnets. The method selects the centroid of the conventional irreducible wedge used in routine band-structure calculations as the representative general k-point, maps it to a spin-flip-related partner, and inserts paired segments through these points into the standard high-symmetry path; these segments systematically sample the interior of the irreducible wedge. We demonstrate the construction for all 54 three-dimensional combinations of extended Bravais lattice type and spin Laue group across the six crystal systems that support collinear altermagnetism, and for the 12 two-dimensional cases spanning the four compatible two-dimensional Bravais lattices. Representative band structures are shown for the distinct lattice/path cases. With AlterSeeK-Path, these band structures can be constructed with essentially the same effort as conventional band structures.

AI.tldr: AlterSeeK-Path is an open-source Python tool that systematically constructs generalized band-structure paths for collinear altermagnets, which exhibit spin splitting but not along conventional high-symmetry paths. The method samples interior points of the irreducible wedge via spin-flip partners and applies to all 54 three-dimensional and 12 two-dimensional compatible lattice/spin Laue group combinations.
AI.motivation: Altermagnetic materials have spin-split band structures with zero net magnetization, but standard high-symmetry k-paths hide this splitting because symmetry lines generally enforce spin degeneracy, making conventional band-structure calculations inadequate for revealing the altermagnetic spin splitting.
AI.method: The method selects the centroid of the conventional irreducible wedge as a representative general k-point, maps it to a spin-flip-related partner, and inserts paired segments through these points into the standard high-symmetry path, systematically sampling the interior of the irreducible wedge.
AI.result: The construction is demonstrated for all 54 three-dimensional combinations of extended Bravais lattice type and spin Laue group across six crystal systems, and for the 12 two-dimensional cases across four compatible Bravais lattices. Representative band structures are shown for distinct lattice/path cases.
AI.conclusion: With AlterSeeK-Path, altermagnetic band structures exhibiting spin splitting can be constructed with essentially the same effort as conventional band structures.

title: First Principle Analysis of the Magnetism and Electronic Structure of Fe2XSi (X=Ti, V)
summary: The electronic, magnetic, and mechanical properties of Fe2XSi, where X is titanium (Ti) and vanadium (V), are investigated using computational methods. Volume optimization reveals that the ground state of Fe2TiSi is a nonmagnetic narrow-band gap semiconductor, and that of Fe2VSi is a ferrimagnetic metal. The negative formation energies of both materials confirm the stability of their crystal structures. Mechanical properties confirm the static stability of the crystal structure and suggest that the titanium compound is ductile; however, the vanadium material is brittle. Density of states and band structure studies confirm the nonmagnetic semiconducting nature with an indirect band gap at Γ and X for the titanium material and the ferrimagnetic-metallic nature of the vanadium material. Electronic and magnetic properties of the materials were investigated with applied tension (negative pressure) and compression (positive pressure) to the crystal structure. The pressure study on Fe2TiSi shows a tunable band gap and a possible semiconductor-metal transition, and Fe2VSi shows a tunable magnetic moment and a possible low-spin/high-spin magnetic transition.

AI.tldr: This paper computationally investigates Fe2TiSi and Fe2VSi full-Heusler alloys. Fe2TiSi is found to be a nonmagnetic narrow-band-gap semiconductor that is ductile, while Fe2VSi is a ferrimagnetic metal that is brittle. Both are stable with negative formation energies. Applied pressure reveals a tunable band gap and possible semiconductor-metal transition in Fe2TiSi, and a tunable magnetic moment with possible low-spin/high-spin transition in Fe2VSi.
AI.motivation: To systematically characterize the electronic, magnetic, and mechanical properties of Fe2XSi (X=Ti, V) compounds and to explore how external pressure (tension and compression) can tune their electronic and magnetic behavior for potential functional applications.
AI.method: Computational (first-principles) methods are employed, including volume optimization, formation energy calculations for structural stability, mechanical property analysis for ductility/brittleness, and density of states (DOS) plus band structure calculations to determine the electronic nature. Pressure is applied as positive (compression) and negative (tension) stress to investigate tunable electronic and magnetic properties.
AI.result: Fe2TiSi is a nonmagnetic narrow-band-gap semiconductor with an indirect band gap at Γ-X and exhibits ductile mechanical behavior. Fe2VSi is a ferrimagnetic metal and is brittle. Both compounds have negative formation energies confirming structural stability. Pressure studies reveal a tunable band gap and possible semiconductor-metal transition in Fe2TiSi, and a tunable magnetic moment with possible low-spin/high-spin transition in Fe2VSi.
AI.conclusion: Fe2TiSi and Fe2VSi are stable Heusler compounds with distinctly different ground states (semiconductor vs. ferrimagnetic metal) and mechanical behavior (ductile vs. brittle). Their electronic and magnetic properties are responsive to applied pressure, offering pathways for gap and magnetic-moment engineering in these materials.

title: Repairing PBE-Spurious Metallicity for HSE06-Level Screening of 2D Photocatalysts for Green Hydrogen Production
summary: Semilocal PBE calculations can remove viable photocatalysts before screening by labeling narrow-gap semiconductors as metals. We address this failure mode in the Computational 2D Materials Database (C2DB) by combining leakage-aware repair of PBE-spurious metallicity with HSE06--PBE $Δ$-learning. Stage~I classifies HSE06-unknown PBE metals using structural, chemical, magnetic, and stability descriptors, while excluding HSE06/GW quantities and PBE electronic shortcuts. Stage~II learns $E_g^{HSE} - E_g^{PBE}$ for the corrected insulating population. The curated XGBoost regressor reconstructs HSE06 gaps with a mean absolute error of 0.108~eV ($R^2=0.989$), compared with 1.036~eV for raw PBE. The Stage~I classifier is used only for triage because the labeled true-metal class contains 29 materials; its best holdout performance gives 87.5\% accuracy, 0.286 true-metal recall, and 0.643 balanced accuracy. The corrected pH~0 electronic screen yields 10 strict and 29 initial relaxed green-hydrogen photocatalyst candidates. Four strict and 18 relaxed candidates would fail the same 1.6--2.8~eV gap window at the PBE level. Targeted VASP HSE06 calculations for six ML-predicted compounds give material-level MAEs of 0.417, 0.182, and 0.110~eV for the C2DB-native, Magpie+structural, and curated models, respectively; \feat{1AgBr-1} shifts above the upper gap cutoff, leaving 28 retained relaxed candidates. The workflow shows that high-fidelity correction must be evaluated by candidate membership, not only by global regression error.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses PBE's spurious metallicity failure in the Computational 2D Materials Database (C2DB) by combining leakage-aware repair of PBE-predicted metals with HSE06-PBE Δ-learning. A Stage-I classifier triages PBE metals, and a curated XGBoost regressor predicts HSE06 band gaps with MAE of 0.108 eV (R²=0.989), dramatically improving over raw PBE (1.036 eV MAE). The corrected electronic screening identifies 10 strict and 29 relaxed green-hydrogen photocatalyst candidates, with several that would be missed via PBE alone. Critically, targeted VASP HSE06 validation reveals that candidate membership—not just global regression error—is the correct metric, as some ML models with good global error still misclassify specific candidates.
AI.motivation: Semilocal PBE calculations erroneously label narrow-gap semiconductors as metals, which can falsely remove viable photocatalysts during computational screening. This failure mode undermines the reliability of high-throughput databases like C2DB for identifying functional materials.
AI.method: The approach combines two stages: (I) a leakage-aware classifier that triages PBE-spurious metals using structural, chemical, magnetic, and stability descriptors (excluding HSE06/GW quantities and PBE electronic shortcuts); and (II) an HSE06−PBE Δ-learning regressor (curated XGBoost) applied to the corrected insulating population to reconstruct accurate band gaps.
AI.result: The curated XGBoost regressor achieves 0.108 eV MAE (R²=0.989) for HSE06 gap reconstruction versus 1.036 eV for raw PBE. The corrected pH=0 electronic screen yields 10 strict and 29 relaxed green-hydrogen photocatalyst candidates, of which 4 strict and 18 relaxed would be missed by PBE gaps. Targeted VASP HSE06 validation gives material-level MAEs of 0.417, 0.182, and 0.110 eV across three models; one compound (1AgBr-1) shifts above the upper gap cutoff, leaving 28 retained relaxed candidates.
AI.conclusion: High-fidelity band-gap correction must be assessed by candidate membership preservation in screening outcomes, not merely by global regression metrics. The leakage-aware curation and model selection choices are decisive for producing reliable photocatalyst shortlists.
